title: Dynamical self-dual criticality in Fibonacci-monitored quantum Ising chains
summary: For the quantum phase transition in the transverse-field Ising chain, Kramers-Wannier duality not only protects its critical properties but also pinpoints the location of the phase transition. Its role in out-of-equilibrium, monitored dynamics, however, remains largely unexplored beyond time-periodic Floquet protocols where self-duality turns into a statistical average symmetry. Here we explore the emergence of dynamical self-duality in the absence of time-translation symmetry by investigating the monitored dynamics of one-dimensional Ising/Majorana chains where measurements are arranged in a quasiperiodic Fibonacci sequence. We find that the dynamical extension of this non-invertible symmetry to an out-of-equilibrium setting allows one to organize the dynamical phase diagram of entangled phases, both predicting the transition locations and protecting universal critical behavior. Analytically and numerically, we identify two distinct critical lines, both related to the golden ratio, for Born-rule weak measurements and for random Clifford projective measurements. The latter coincides with the transition of a pure imaginary-time evolution, which can be viewed as a post-selected trajectory. The universality classes of the long-time critical steady states at Fibonacci times are determined, while the transient dynamics between Fibonacci times is deformed by measurements, realizing dynamical measurement-altered quantum criticality in real time.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how Kramers-Wannier duality emerges in out-of-equilibrium monitored quantum dynamics of Ising/Majorana chains with quasiperiodic Fibonacci measurement sequences, identifying two distinct critical lines tied to the golden ratio that govern entanglement phase transitions and universal critical behavior.
AI.motivation: While Kramers-Wannier duality is well-understood for equilibrium quantum phase transitions and time-periodic Floquet systems, its role in out-of-equilibrium monitored dynamics without time-translation symmetry remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors investigate monitored dynamics of one-dimensional Ising/Majorana chains with measurements arranged in a quasiperiodic Fibonacci sequence, using both analytical and numerical approaches for Born-rule weak measurements and random Clifford projective measurements.
AI.result: Two distinct critical lines are identified, both related to the golden ratio. For Born-rule weak measurements and random Clifford projective measurements, the critical lines govern entanglement phase transitions. The Clifford case coincides with a transition of pure imaginary-time evolution interpretable as a post-selected trajectory.
AI.conclusion: The dynamical extension of non-invertible symmetry to out-of-equilibrium settings organizes the dynamical phase diagram of entangled phases, predicting transition locations and protecting universal critical behavior. The universality classes of long-time critical steady states at Fibonacci times are determined, with transient dynamics exhibiting dynamical measurement-altered quantum criticality.

title: Bit flips, saturation, and quantum chaos in dissipative cat qubits
summary: Bosonic cat qubits promise hardware-efficient quantum error correction because their logical bit-flip rate is exponentially suppressed with the photon number of the cat state. However, several experiments report a saturation of this suppression at large photon numbers, thus limiting the achievable protection. Combining quantum-trajectory simulations, semiclassical analysis, and Liouvillian spectral methods, we investigate the properties of bit flips in realistic dissipative cat qubits, where a memory mode hosting quantum information interacts with a dissipative buffer cavity. We show that bit flips are dynamical processes inherently involving both the memory and buffer, and therefore cannot be captured by single-mode approximate descriptions. We identify a reflection symmetry, resulting in a phase-locking condition at the semiclassical level and for quantum trajectories, as the main requirement for regular bit-flip dynamics. Its breakdown is the origin of the saturation, and we find that it occurs when two conditions are met. First, the adiabatic approximation, where the state of the buffer instantaneously follows that of the memory, must not be valid, which typically happens at large photon numbers. Second, key parameters such as the cross-Kerr interaction and dephasing must be present, leading to irregular dynamics in which memory fluctuations are amplified by the buffer during bit flips. In this regime, we find that bit flips manifest as chaotic bursts within otherwise regular dynamics, as evidenced by both changes in the topology of quantum trajectories and in the Liouvillian spectrum and its associated eigenmodes involved in these switching events. Finally, we verify our predictions against experimental data, highlighting the detrimental role of dissipative chaotic behavior in bosonic error-correcting codes.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the saturation of bit-flip suppression at large photon numbers in bosonic cat qubits, identifying that bit flips are dynamical processes involving both memory and buffer modes. The breakdown of a reflection symmetry (phase-locking condition) causes saturation, occurring when adiabatic approximation fails and when cross-Kerr interaction and dephasing are present, leading to chaotic bursts in bit-flip dynamics.
AI.motivation: Bosonic cat qubits promise exponential suppression of logical bit-flip errors, but experiments show saturation at large photon numbers, limiting performance. The authors aim to understand the physical origin of this saturation to enable better error correction.
AI.method: Combined quantum-trajectory simulations, semiclassical analysis, and Liouvillian spectral methods to study bit flips in realistic dissipative cat qubits with a memory mode interacting with a dissipative buffer cavity.
AI.result: Bit flips are inherently two-mode (memory+buffer) dynamical processes; saturation originates from breakdown of a reflection symmetry/phase-locking condition when (1) adiabatic approximation fails (large photon numbers) and (2) cross-Kerr interaction and dephasing are present, causing chaotic bursts in bit-flip dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Dissipative chaotic behavior in bosonic error-correcting codes is detrimental; verified against experimental data.

title: Bell State Analysis Provides an Optimal Basis Saturating the Quantum Cramer-Rao in Rotation Sensing
summary: The second-order anti-coherent state of light is known to saturate the Cramer-Rao Bound (QCRB) for rotation sensing around an arbitrary axis. However, due to the complexity of the state and the inefficiency of state tomography, parameter extraction remains an open problem. In this manuscript, we approach the problem of parameter extraction using pair-wise Bell state analysis with an additional path degree of freedom. Due to the transformation property of rotation, only the symmetric Bell states will show up in projection in the final state. We exploit this advantage to develop a scheme for extracting the rotation angle for N=4 and N=6 second-order anti-coherent states.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses parameter extraction from second-order anti-coherent states for rotation sensing by using pair-wise Bell state analysis with an additional path degree of freedom, developing schemes to extract rotation angles for N=4 and N=6 states.
AI.motivation: Second-order anti-coherent states saturate the QCRB for rotation sensing, but parameter extraction remains challenging due to state complexity and inefficient tomography.
AI.method: The approach uses pair-wise Bell state analysis with an additional path degree of freedom, exploiting the property that only symmetric Bell states appear in projection under rotation transformations.
AI.result: Schemes for extracting rotation angles were developed for N=4 and N=6 second-order anti-coherent states.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Bell state analysis method provides a viable avenue for parameter extraction from anti-coherent states, overcoming limitations of full state tomography.

title: Quantum Sensing and Quantum Error Correction: Two Sides of the Same Coin
summary: Quantum metrology has been making amazing progress in the past decades. It is always in researchers' interest to search for new optimal states that improve parameter estimation. In this paper, we point out a connection between the code's error correcting capacity and its ability to act as a sensor. We backed our claim by providing an example that relates the Absorption emission code to the sensor state for arbitrary state rotation. It is hoped that, in building such a unified theory, one can draw inspiration from error correction to develop promising quantum sensors.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a connection between quantum error-correcting codes and quantum metrology, showing that the error-correcting capacity of a code determines its ability to act as a quantum sensor, demonstrated through the Absorption Emission code for arbitrary state rotation.
AI.motivation: To find new optimal states for improved parameter estimation in quantum metrology by exploring the relationship between error-correcting codes and sensing capabilities.
AI.method: The authors theoretically demonstrate a connection between a code's error-correcting capacity and its sensor performance, using the Absorption Emission code as an example for arbitrary state rotation sensing.
AI.result: A direct relationship is established between error correction capacity and sensing ability, validated through the Absorption Emission code example.
AI.conclusion: The unified theory allows researchers to leverage error correction techniques to develop promising quantum sensors, providing a new pathway for quantum metrology advancement.

title: Anderson Localization: A Floquet operator Krylov space perspective
summary: The problem of Anderson localization, as well as the single particle localization-delocalizaton transition of the Aubry-André model, is studied employing operator Krylov space methods. It is shown that even when the dynamics is generated by a Hamiltonian, studying the dynamics at stroboscopic rather than continuous times has its advantages. In particular, mapping the dynamics to an effective Floquet problem results in an operator Krylov space description where quantities such as the spectral function can be computed with fewer computational resources, while a moment method exists that allows for the extraction of Krylov parameters directly from the discrete time autocorrelation function. For stroboscopic dynamics, the operator Krylov space corresponds to the dynamics of an edge operator of an inhomogeneous Floquet transverse field Ising model, with the parameters of this effective model generated recursively. The Krylov parameters show disorder-averaged renormalization with their distribution narrowing as the recursion step increases. It is shown that a more physical spectral function is obtained from the Krylov parameters obtained from the disorder-averaged autocorrelation function, rather than the disorder-averaged Krylov parameters. The delocalized (localized) phase is shown to correspond to the appearance (absence) of a Porter-Thomas distribution, a ballistically propagating (localized) wavefront in operator Krylov space, and a smooth (discrete) Berstein-Szegö power-spectrum. The localization-delocalization transition is also demonstrated in operator Krylov space. A Porter-Thomas distribution is also observed at the critical point. The long-time dynamics and the inverse participation ratio at the critical point is shown to exhibit behavior consistent with a multi-fractal scaling with system size.

AI.tldr: This paper studies Anderson localization and the Aubry-André model using operator Krylov space methods, showing advantages of stroboscopic over continuous-time dynamics, mapping to an effective Floquet transverse field Ising model, and characterizing localization-delocalization transitions via Porter-Thomas distributions, ballistic vs. localized wavefronts, and Bernstein-Szegö spectra, with multifractal scaling at the critical point.
AI.motivation: To study Anderson localization and the single-particle localization-delocalization transition of the Aubry-André model using operator Krylov space methods, and to demonstrate the advantages of stroboscopic dynamics over continuous-time dynamics in this context.
AI.method: Operator Krylov space methods are employed with stroboscopic dynamics mapped to an effective Floquet problem. A moment method extracts Krylov parameters from discrete-time autocorrelation functions. Disorder-averaged quantities are analyzed, and the dynamics are mapped to an edge operator of an inhomogeneous Floquet transverse field Ising model.
AI.result: The delocalized phase exhibits a Porter-Thomas distribution, ballistically propagating wavefront, and smooth Bernstein-Szegö spectrum; the localized phase shows absence of Porter-Thomas, localized wavefront, and discrete spectrum. A Porter-Thomas distribution also appears at the critical point. The critical point shows multifractal scaling in long-time dynamics and inverse participation ratio.
AI.conclusion: Operator Krylov space methods with stroboscopic dynamics provide an efficient framework for studying localization-delocalization transitions, with disorder-averaged autocorrelation functions yielding more physical spectral functions than disorder-averaged Krylov parameters.

title: Phase-resolved multichannel quantum escape between limit cycles
summary: Driven-dissipative quantum systems can recover stable dynamical attractors in the semiclassical limit, including coexisting limit cycles. At finite fluctuation strength, this classical coexistence becomes quantum metastability: the corresponding oscillatory states undergo rare fluctuation-induced transitions. We demonstrate phase-resolved quantum escape between two such states in a driven optomechanical resonator. Unlike escape from fixed points, switching between extended attractors occurs across a periodic basin boundary and depends on the phase at which fluctuations approach it. Using quantum-jump trajectories across a controlled quantum-to-classical crossover, we reconstruct the escape geometry directly from switching events. Escape from the small-amplitude cycle proceeds through a single radial corridor and exhibits near-Arrhenius scaling, whereas escape from the large-amplitude cycle involves competing phase-localized corridors with distinct effective activation scales. The resulting curvature in the switching-rate scaling, together with event-conditioned phase distributions, identifies finite-fluctuation multichannel quantum escape between extended attractors.

AI.tldr: This paper studies phase-resolved quantum escape between coexisting limit cycles in a driven optomechanical resonator, revealing multichannel escape dynamics with distinct activation scales depending on the phase of fluctuations.
AI.motivation: To understand how quantum metastability and rare fluctuation-induced transitions occur between coexisting limit cycles in driven-dissipative quantum systems, extending escape theory from fixed points to extended attractors.
AI.method: Using quantum-jump trajectories across a controlled quantum-to-classical crossover in a driven optomechanical resonator, reconstructing escape geometry directly from switching events with phase resolution.
AI.result: Escape from the small-amplitude cycle proceeds through a single radial corridor with near-Arrhenius scaling; escape from the large-amplitude cycle involves competing phase-localized corridors with distinct effective activation scales, producing curvature in switching-rate scaling.
AI.conclusion: Finite-fluctuation multichannel quantum escape between extended attractors is identified via event-conditioned phase distributions, demonstrating phase-dependent escape that differs fundamentally from fixed-point escape.

title: Lateral Shift as a Control Knob for Localization Transitions in a Quasiperiodic Ladder
summary: This work reports rich localization-delocalization transitions in a quasiperiodic ladder, of which the two legs are subject to the same quasiperiodic onsite potential but can be shifted laterally relative to each other. It is found that the lateral shift between the two legs effectively generates a magnetic flux in the reciprocal momentum space. The lateral shift thus offers a control knob, allowing us to access and simulate rich phenomena including magnetic-flux-enhanced localization, magnetic-flux-suppressed localization, and magnetic-flux-induced reentrant localization transitions. The underlying physical mechanisms as well as the phase boundaries separating localized, mixed, and extended phases are both qualitatively and quantitatively understood, based on a band-structure analysis that employs a commensurate approximation to the quasiperiodic potential, requiring only unit cells of small to modest sizes. Our work provides a highly tunable platform for exploring localization physics with promising applications such as quantum switching, and a broadly applicable approach for understanding localization-delocalization transitions in quasiperiodic systems.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates localization-delocalization transitions in a quasiperiodic ladder with a lateral shift between legs, which effectively generates a magnetic flux in reciprocal space. The shift enables control over magnetic-flux-enhanced/suppressed localization and reentrant transitions. A band-structure analysis with commensurate approximation explains the phase boundaries. The work offers a tunable platform for localization physics and quantum switching applications.
AI.motivation: To explore how lateral shifts in a quasiperiodic ladder create effective magnetic fluxes in reciprocal momentum space, enabling controlled manipulation of localization-delocalization transitions beyond conventional settings.
AI.method: The authors study a quasiperiodic ladder with identical onsite potentials on both legs but with a tunable lateral shift. They employ a band-structure analysis using a commensurate approximation to the quasiperiodic potential, requiring only small to modest unit cell sizes, to qualitatively and quantitatively understand phase boundaries.
AI.result: The lateral shift effectively generates a magnetic flux in reciprocal momentum space. This leads to magnetic-flux-enhanced localization, magnetic-flux-suppressed localization, and magnetic-flux-induced reentrant localization transitions. Phase boundaries separating localized, mixed, and extended phases are identified.
AI.conclusion: The quasiperiodic ladder with lateral shift provides a highly tunable platform for exploring rich localization physics and enables applications like quantum switching. The commensurate approximation approach is broadly applicable to understanding localization-delocalization transitions in quasiperiodic systems.

title: Impact of Surface Treatment on Noise in PL-Measurements of Silicon Vacancies in 4H-SiC Lateral pin-Diodes
comment: 38 pages (main text and SI), 8 figures, published in Nano Letters
summary: Silicon vacancies ($V_\mathrm{Si}$) in 4H-SiC are promising candidates for quantum technologies due to their long spin coherence times and integrability into mature semiconductor platforms. However, conventional CMOS-compatible processing introduces significant photoluminescence noise from passivation layers and crystal damage, degrading color center coherence and excitation linewidths. This work evaluates strategies to minimize such background noise. Thermally grown oxides with nitrogen monoxide annealing provide excellent low-noise passivation, remaining stable during subsequent $600\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ thermal treatments. Furthermore, combining reactive ion etching with atomic layer etching eliminates ion-induced surface damage. Into lateral pin-diodes, used for stark shift and photoluminescent excitation linewidth tuning, a selectively etched optical window is integrated. These devices show ideal electrical properties -- blocking up to $150\,\mathrm{V}$ with leakage current below $10\,\mathrm{pA}/μ\mathrm{m}$ -- while significantly enhancing the $V_\mathrm{Si}$ environment. Single emitters in these pin-diodes show an increased signal-to-noise ratio of 15 for near-surface and of 50 for deeper emitters on both c-plane and a-plane wafers.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates strategies to reduce photoluminescence noise in 4H-SiC silicon vacancies by optimizing CMOS-compatible processing, achieving low-noise passivation (thermally grown oxides with NO annealing) and damage-free etching (RIE+ALE), integrated into pin-diodes with selectively etched optical windows. Resulting devices show excellent electrical properties and significantly improved signal-to-noise ratios (15 for near-surface, 50 for deeper emitters).
AI.motivation: Silicon vacancies in 4H-SiC are promising for quantum technologies but conventional CMOS-compatible processing introduces photoluminescence noise from passivation layers and crystal damage, degrading coherence and excitation linewidths. The motivation is to minimize this background noise.
AI.method: Evaluated thermally grown oxides with nitrogen monoxide (NO) annealing for low-noise passivation stable up to 600°C; combined reactive ion etching (RIE) with atomic layer etching (ALE) to eliminate ion-induced surface damage; integrated selectively etched optical windows into lateral pin-diodes for Stark shift and photoluminescent excitation linewidth tuning.
AI.result: Devices block up to 150 V with leakage current below 10 pA/μm, showing ideal electrical properties. Single emitters achieved signal-to-noise ratio of 15 for near-surface and 50 for deeper emitters on both c-plane and a-plane wafers.
AI.conclusion: CMOS-compatible processing can be optimized to significantly enhance the V_Si environment in 4H-SiC pin-diodes, improving signal-to-noise ratios for quantum applications.

title: Topological metal-insulator transitions in one-dimensional non-Hermitian quasicrystals: beyond PT-symmetry
summary: One-dimensional non-Hermitian quasicrystals with parity and time-reversal (PT) symmetry can simultaneously exhibit localization-delocalization transition, topological phase transition, and PT-symmetry-breaking transition. This motivates this work to investigate how the absence of PT symmetry impacts topological metal-insulator transitions in non-Hermitian quasicrystals. We propose a non-Hermitian quasiperiodic model that generally does not preserve PT symmetry and demonstrate that, in most parameter regions, such a system supports triple phase transitions that encompass localization, topology, and degeneracy-breaking. The system may also exhibit a particular type of localization-delocalization transition analogous to the Hermitian case, namely, without activating topological phase transitions or degeneracy-breaking transitions. Our work extends the topological metal-insulator transitions previously studied in PT-symmetric systems to a more general class of non-Hermitian setting, and further reveals that non-Hermitian systems can host distinct types of localization behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the study of topological metal-insulator transitions from PT-symmetric to general non-Hermitian quasicrystals, demonstrating that most parameter regions support triple phase transitions (localization, topology, degeneracy-breaking), while some regions exhibit Hermitian-like localization-delocalization transitions without topological or degeneracy changes.
AI.motivation: To investigate how the absence of PT symmetry impacts topological metal-insulator transitions in non-Hermitian quasicrystals, motivated by the fact that PT-symmetric systems exhibit simultaneous localization, topological, and PT-breaking transitions.
AI.method: Proposing a non-Hermitian quasiperiodic model that generally lacks PT symmetry and analyzing its phase transitions across different parameter regions.
AI.result: The system supports triple phase transitions (localization, topology, degeneracy-breaking) in most parameter regions, and also exhibits a Hermitian-like localization-delocalization transition without topological or degeneracy-breaking transitions in certain parameter regions.
AI.conclusion: The work extends topological metal-insulator transitions from PT-symmetric to more general non-Hermitian systems, revealing distinct types of localization behavior in non-Hermitian quasicrystals.

title: Optimal Quantum Differential Privacy via Fisher Information Spectral Analysis
summary: The Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) metric governs a fundamental duality: it quantifies both how precisely a parameter can be estimated (metrology) and how distinguishable two quantum states are (privacy). We exploit this duality to establish a geometry-aware framework for quantum differential privacy (DP) that replaces isotropic depolarizing noise with direction-dependent noise aligned to the QFI eigenstructure of the quantum embedding. We prove six principal theorems: (1) the minimax-optimal mechanism concentrates the noise budget in the dominant QFI eigenmode, achieving $\varepsilon = (Δ^2/2)λ_{\max}(1-cγ)$ with $O(d/λ_{\max})$ advantage; (2) mixed-state QFI decomposition reveals that dephasing in the adversary's basis $\textit{increases}$ accessible information, while misaligned-basis dephasing provides constructive privacy amplification from hardware noise; (3) a tight privacy $-$ utility uncertainty relation $\varepsilon \cdot (1 - F) \ge \frac{Δ^2}{2}\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(F)}{d}$; (4) adaptive QFI estimation converging at $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ yields $1.92\times$ tighter bounds; (5) QFI-aligned composition saturates at $O(1)$ versus $O(k)$ for standard composition; and (6) hardware noise can be harnessed for privacy amplification. Adversarial vulnerabilities, Wasserstein guarantees, subspace projection, and a zero-knowledge audit protocol follow as corollaries. Results are validated on Qiskit Aer GPU simulations, IBM Quantum hardware (ibm_fez, 156 qubits), and against classical DP baselines, achieving equivalent utility at $\varepsilon \approx 0.001$ versus $\varepsilon \approx 4800$ for classical DP.

AI.tldr: A geometry-aware quantum differential privacy framework using QFI-aligned anisotropic noise achieves ε ≈ 0.001 (vs. ε ≈ 4800 for classical DP) through six theorems on optimal noise allocation, mixed-state QFI, uncertainty relations, adaptive estimation, composition, and hardware noise amplification.
AI.motivation: To replace isotropic depolarizing noise in quantum DP with direction-dependent noise aligned to the QFI eigenstructure, exploiting the duality between quantum metrology (parameter estimation precision) and privacy (state distinguishability) for improved privacy-utility tradeoffs.
AI.method: Develops a QFI-geometry-aware framework with anisotropic noise aligned to the QFI eigenstructure; proves six principal theorems covering minimax-optimal mechanisms, mixed-state QFI decomposition, privacy-utility uncertainty relations, adaptive QFI estimation, composition properties, and hardware noise exploitation; validated on Qiskit Aer GPU and IBM Quantum hardware (ibm_fez, 156 qubits).
AI.result: Achieves ε ≈ 0.001 vs. ε ≈ 4800 for classical DP at equivalent utility; 1.92× tighter bounds via adaptive QFI estimation; O(1) vs. O(k) composition saturation; constructive privacy amplification from hardware dephasing noise.
AI.conclusion: QFI-aligned anisotropic noise dramatically outperforms classical isotropic DP baselines, and hardware noise can be harnessed rather than mitigated for quantum privacy amplification.

title: Sensitivity to perturbations in the three-dimensional Anderson model
summary: We investigate the fidelity susceptibility, which quantifies the sensitivity of single-particle eigenstates to perturbations, in the three-dimensional Anderson model. As a function of disorder strength $W$, it exhibits two distinct peaks. The first peak signals a crossover at weak disorder strength from plane-wave states to single-particle quantum chaos, and its position shifts toward $W\to 0$ in the thermodynamic limit. The second peak emerges, to high numerical accuracy, at the critical disorder strength associated with the Anderson localization transition. We further show that the divergence of the first peak is maximal, scaling as the square of the inverse frequency cutoff, whereas the divergence of the second peak is submaximal. We relate the latter suppression to the fractal structure of single-particle eigenstates at criticality. We discuss two distinct scenarios that give rise to the peaks in the fidelity susceptibilities. Moreover, studying the scaling of typical fidelity susceptibilities above the Anderson transition, we find evidence of two distinct regimes of nonergodic behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates fidelity susceptibility in the 3D Anderson model, finding two distinct peaks: one signaling a crossover to quantum chaos (first peak) and another marking the Anderson localization transition (second peak). The first peak diverges maximally, while the second shows submaximal divergence linked to fractal eigenstate structure. Evidence of two nonergodic regimes above the transition is also found.
AI.motivation: To understand how single-particle eigenstates respond to perturbations across the Anderson localization transition, and to characterize quantum chaos and nonergodic behavior in disordered systems using fidelity susceptibility as a probe.
AI.method: Numerical analysis of fidelity susceptibility in the three-dimensional Anderson model, examining its scaling behavior as a function of disorder strength W, including peak positions, divergence exponents, and typical susceptibility scaling above the transition.
AI.result: Two peaks are observed: the first (weak disorder) shifts to W→0 in the thermodynamic limit and diverges maximally (scaling as inverse frequency cutoff squared); the second aligns with the Anderson critical disorder and shows submaximal divergence. Two distinct nonergodic regimes are identified above the transition.
AI.conclusion: Fidelity susceptibility captures both the crossover to single-particle quantum chaos and the Anderson localization transition. The submaximal divergence at criticality is tied to fractal eigenstate structure, and nonergodic extended states exist in two distinct regimes above the transition.

title: Towards Scalable Quaternary Message-Passing Decoding for Quantum Error Correction
summary: The scalability and interpretability of message-passing (MP) decoding, such as (quaternary) Belief Propagation, remain open challenges in quantum error correction. Even for surface codes, arguably the first testbed for decoding methods, studies of improved MP decoders have mostly been restricted to small distances ($d \lesssim 19$). Moreover, the mismatch with established message-passing theory limits the decoder's interpretability, making it unclear whether MP decoding can sustain its effectiveness at large system sizes. This work takes a step toward a more principled and interpretable MP decoding framework, with the goal of making MP-based decoding more reliable and bridging theory and practice. We introduce a dilution method, which allows a quaternary Min-Sum (MS) decoder to exhibit an apparent depolarizing threshold of $16\%$ up to distance $20$, outperforming Minimum-Weight Perfect Matching in finite-length regimes. Notably, for $X$-noise, the standard MS decoder under dilution has worst-case complexity $O(N \log^2 d)$ and outperforms BP-OSD at $d=65$. The observed $\sim 9\%$ threshold may correspond to a true asymptotic threshold. Finally, we give a graph-dilution argument that interprets the success of the dilution method and offers insight into when MP algorithms can genuinely scale. Taken together, these results provide encouraging progress toward scalable and interpretable MP decoding in quantum error correction.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a dilution method for quaternary Min-Sum decoding that achieves a 16% depolarizing threshold up to distance 20, outperforms MWPM in finite-length regimes, and for X-noise achieves worst-case O(N log² d) complexity while outperforming BP-OSD at d=65, with a graph-dilution argument providing theoretical interpretability for MP decoding scalability.
AI.motivation: Scalability and interpretability of message-passing (MP) decoding in quantum error correction remain open challenges, with improved MP decoders largely restricted to small distances (d ≤ 19) and a mismatch with established MP theory making it unclear whether MP decoding can sustain effectiveness at large system sizes.
AI.method: The authors introduce a dilution method applied to a quaternary Min-Sum (MS) decoder, along with a graph-dilution argument that interprets the method's success and offers insight into when MP algorithms can genuinely scale.
AI.result: The diluted quaternary MS decoder exhibits an apparent depolarizing threshold of 16% up to distance 20, outperforming MWPM in finite-length regimes. Under X-noise, the standard MS decoder with dilution has worst-case complexity O(N log² d) and outperforms BP-OSD at d=65, with an observed ~9% threshold possibly corresponding to a true asymptotic threshold.
AI.conclusion: The results provide encouraging progress toward scalable and interpretable MP decoding in quantum error correction, bridging theory and practice.

title: Spectral properties of non-Hermitian real random matrices with long-range correlations
comment: 7 pages, 6 figures, accepted at Phys. Rev. E
summary: We investigate the spectral properties of non-Hermitian real random matrices whose entries exhibit long-range correlations decaying as~$|r-r'|^{-α}$. We find a progressive breakdown of the circular law, controlled by the decrease of~$α$. In all cases, the radial eigenvalue density decreases away from the origin. At~$α>1$, an effective radius, reminiscent of the circular law, is retrieved, while instead, for~$α<1$, the eigenvalue distribution broadens with matrix size and its spectral radius grows like a power law, with exponents numerically close to the exponents controlling the magnitude of fluctuations in the extended central limit theorem. The case~$α=1$ appears as a case with self-similar eigenvalue density, and slowly growing spectral radius. Long-range correlations also enhance clustering of real eigenvalues and slow the resorption of the Saturn effect. These results reveal a correlation-driven transition and suggest the emergence of a new universality class for correlated non-Hermitian random matrices.

AI.tldr: This paper studies non-Hermitian random matrices with long-range correlated entries (decaying as |r-r'|^{-α}) and finds a transition in spectral properties controlled by α: for α>1, behavior reminiscent of the circular law persists; for α<1, the spectral radius grows as a power law with exponents linked to the extended central limit theorem; α=1 is a self-similar critical case. Long-range correlations also enhance real eigenvalue clustering and slow the Saturn effect, suggesting a new universality class.
AI.motivation: To understand how long-range correlations in matrix entries affect the spectral properties of non-Hermitian random matrices, beyond the standard independent-entry assumption underlying the circular law.
AI.method: The authors investigate non-Hermitian real random matrices with entries that have long-range correlations decaying as a power law |r-r'|^{-α}. They analyze the eigenvalue density, spectral radius scaling, and eigenvalue clustering as functions of α.
AI.result: A transition at α=1 is found: α>1 recovers an effective radius reminiscent of the circular law; α<1 yields a broadening eigenvalue distribution with spectral radius growing as a power law with exponents close to those of the extended central limit theorem; α=1 exhibits self-similar eigenvalue density and slowly growing spectral radius. Long-range correlations increase real eigenvalue clustering and slow the resorption of the Saturn effect.
AI.conclusion: Long-range correlations drive a transition in the spectral statistics of non-Hermitian random matrices, suggesting a new universality class distinct from the standard circular law ensemble.

title: Quantum-Adaptive KS($\varphi$): A Parameterized Three-Qubit Gate Family Embedding Toffoli with Measurement-Free Phase Kickback and Intrinsic Error Non-Amplification
summary: We introduce Quantum-Adaptive KS($\varphi$) ($K$ = kickback, $S$ = sandwich), a parameterized three-qubit gate family that structurally embeds the Toffoli (CCX) gate within two additional components: (1)a palindromic Hadamard sandwich on the first control qubit $q_0$ that conjugates $Z$-type errors to $X$-type in the CCX frame, providing simultaneous sensitivity to both error types without ancilla overhead; and (2)a controlled-phase (CP) gate whose quantum phase kickback propagates post-CCX target-state information into the control-qubit phase without measurement. The term Quantum- Adaptive refers to amplitude steering conditioned by the compile-time parameter $\varphi$ via a Quantum Neural Cellular Automaton (QNCA) majority-inspired bias rule; the gate does not self-modify at runtime. Two QA-KS($π$) gates chained on a shared control qubit $q_0$ produce outputs completely orthogonal to two sequential CCX gates on $q_0$=1 inputs (output fidelity F=0.000), while agreeing exactly on $q_0$=0 inputs (F=1.000). This subspace-dependent divergence is the direct computational signature of coherent phase retention across gate boundaries -- impossible for CCX-only circuits. On the $q_1$ = 0 subspace the gate acts deterministically (up to a relative phase), providing intrinsic error non-amplification. On the $q_1$ = 1 subspace it produces four-component entangled superpositions, making it a strictly distinct quantum-native primitive from CCX. We present the complete $8 \times 8$ unitary matrix, confirmed exact to $||U^{\dagger}U-I||_{\infty} < 10^{-15}$, and define two canonical variants: QA-KS$_{π/2}$ ($\varphi = π/2$, $S$ gate) and QA-KS$_π$ ($\varphi = π$, $Z$ gate). Qiskit depolarizing-noise simulation demonstrates near-unit fidelity at $p \leq 10^{-2}$ with an honest depth cost at higher error rates. The gate preserves the three-qubit footprint of CCX with no qubit overhead.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces QA-KS(φ)—a parameterized three-qubit gate that embeds a Toffoli gate with a Hadamard sandwich and a controlled-phase gate, enabling dual error-type sensitivity and coherent phase propagation without ancilla overhead. Two chained QA-KS(π) gates produce orthogonal outputs on |1⟩ inputs and identical outputs on |0⟩ inputs, demonstrating novel quantum-native behavior beyond CCX.
AI.motivation: To design a three-qubit quantum gate that goes beyond the Toffoli (CCX) gate by providing simultaneous sensitivity to Z-type and X-type errors, enabling coherent phase retention across gate boundaries, and achieving subspace-dependent divergence without ancilla overhead.
AI.method: The gate structurally embeds a Toffoli (CCX) gate with: (1) a palindromic Hadamard sandwich on the first control qubit to conjugate Z-errors to X-type in the CCX frame, and (2) a controlled-phase (CP) gate using quantum phase kickback. A compile-time parameter φ controls amplitude steering via a QNCA majority-inspired bias rule. The gate is validated via the complete 8×8 unitary matrix (||U†U−I||∞<10^−15) and Qiskit depolarizing-noise simulations.
AI.result: Two chained QA-KS(π) gates on a shared control qubit produce completely orthogonal outputs on |1⟩ inputs (fidelity F=0.000) and exact agreement on |0⟩ inputs (F=1.000). On the |q₁=0⟩ subspace the gate acts deterministically up to a relative phase (error non-amplification), while on |q₁=1⟩ subspace it produces four-component entangled superpositions. Qiskit simulations show near-unit fidelity at p≤10^−2.
AI.conclusion: QA-KS(φ) is a strictly distinct quantum-native primitive from CCX, preserving the three-qubit footprint with no qubit overhead, enabling coherent phase retention and dual error-type sensitivity. Two canonical variants are defined: QA-KS_{π/2} (S gate) and QA-KS_π (Z gate).

title: Cluster moves with an entropic reservoir accelerate low-temperature simulations of three-dimensional spin glasses
summary: We present an algorithm for the simulation of three-dimensional spin glasses deep in the low-temperature phase: Parallel Tempering enhanced with Houdayer moves and with an entropic reservoir (PTHR). Although differences with the standard Houdayer algorithm are small, PTHR allows us to equilibrate a large number of samples of $L=16$ lattices with Gaussian couplings for temperatures $T\geq 0.2$. We show that the computational complexity displays better size scaling than standard Parallel Tempering. For finite sizes, our method outperforms other cluster algorithms by a speedup factor of around 64. In close analogy with standard Parallel Tempering, PTHR's computational complexity strongly relates to temperature chaos.

AI.tldr: PTHR, an enhanced Parallel Tempering algorithm with Houdayer moves and entropic reservoir, outperforms standard methods for simulating 3D spin glasses at low temperatures, achieving 64x speedup and better size scaling.
AI.motivation: To efficiently simulate three-dimensional spin glasses deep in the low-temperature phase, addressing the poor size scaling of standard Parallel Tempering algorithms.
AI.method: Parallel Tempering enhanced with Houdayer moves and an entropic reservoir (PTHR), applied to L=16 lattices with Gaussian couplings at T≥0.2.
AI.result: PTHR equilibrates many samples efficiently, achieves 64x speedup over other cluster algorithms, and exhibits better computational complexity scaling than standard Parallel Tempering.
AI.conclusion: PTHR's computational complexity is strongly tied to temperature chaos, analogous to standard Parallel Tempering, and it significantly outperforms existing methods for finite-size spin glass simulations.

title: Self-Generated Chiral Rotation in Whispering-Gallery Optomechanics
summary: Backscattering in whispering-gallery-mode resonators is usually a passive mode-splitting mechanism produced by a fixed defect. Here, we show that, when the backscatterer is a mechanical angular degree of freedom, the same process becomes an angular-recoil backaction channel capable of generating chirality under reciprocal driving. A localized movable scatterer coherently converts photons between clockwise and counterclockwise whispering-gallery modes, transferring angular recoil in each circulation-changing event. In a weak-scattering driven-dissipative model, reciprocal bidirectional pumping gives zero net torque at rest, but rotation Doppler-shifts the two opposite scattering rates in opposite directions. For suitable detuning, this feedback produces negative angular friction, destabilizes the nonrotating reciprocal state, and selects one of two symmetry-related steady rotations. The threshold scales inversely with the square of the WGM azimuthal index. The mechanically chiral state produces a direction-dependent weak-probe response, visible as a Doppler splitting of the backscattered spectra, turning passive WGM mode splitting into a minimal mechanism for autonomous chiral optomechanics.

AI.tldr: A movable scatterer in a whispering-gallery-mode resonator can create chirality via angular recoil, causing spontaneous rotation due to negative angular friction, even under reciprocal driving.
AI.motivation: To show that a mechanical backscatterer (angular degree of freedom) in WGM resonators can turn passive mode splitting into an active, autonomous chiral optomechanical system.
AI.method: Weak-scattering driven-dissipative model where a movable scatterer couples clockwise and counterclockwise WGMs. Rotation Doppler-shifts scattering rates, leading to negative angular friction and spontaneous symmetry breaking.
AI.result: Reciprocal bidirectional pumping yields zero net torque at rest, but rotation induces feedback that destabilizes the nonrotating state and selects one of two steady rotations. Threshold scales inversely with the square of the WGM azimuthal index. Chirality manifests as Doppler-split backscattered spectra.
AI.conclusion: This provides a minimal mechanism for autonomous chiral optomechanics, converting passive WGM mode splitting into a chiral response under reciprocal driving.

title: Digital twins for compact hybrid quantum classical learning in FMCW radar detection
summary: Frequency-modulated continuous-wave radar sensing often relies on labeled measurements that are costly, restricted, or difficult to collect at scale. This work evaluates physics-informed digital twins as controlled testbeds for early-stage quantum-classical radar learning. Two synthetic radar benchmarks are considered: unmanned aerial vehicle classification from range-Doppler maps and human fall detection from Doppler-time spectrograms. For both tasks, inputs are standardized, reduced using principal component analysis, and classified using either a radial basis function support vector classifier or a quantum support vector classifier. All quantum-kernel results are obtained using noiseless classical simulation; no quantum hardware is used, and no quantum-advantage claim is made. Across five random seeds, the quantum support vector classifier improves the UAV benchmark from four principal components onward, reaching an accuracy of 0.941 +/- 0.012 at eight components, compared with 0.880 +/- 0.029 for the classical baseline. On the fall-detection benchmark, both classifiers perform similarly, with a small quantum-kernel improvement at higher feature dimensions. A Gaussian-noise robustness study shows limited performance degradation across the tested noise levels, while preserving the UAV quantum-kernel gain. These results support digital twins as useful, controlled environments for radar-QML benchmarking prior to measured-data validation and hardware execution.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates physics-informed digital twins as controlled testbeds for quantum-classical radar learning, showing that quantum support vector classifiers outperform classical baselines on UAV classification (0.941 vs 0.880 accuracy) while performing similarly on fall detection, with robustness to Gaussian noise.
AI.motivation: Labeled measurements for frequency-modulated continuous-wave radar sensing are costly, restricted, or difficult to collect at scale, motivating the need for alternative training environments like digital twins.
AI.method: Two synthetic radar benchmarks (UAV classification from range-Doppler maps and fall detection from Doppler-time spectrograms) are processed with PCA dimensionality reduction and classified using radial basis function support vector classifier (SVC) vs. quantum SVC on noiseless classical simulation.
AI.result: Quantum SVC achieved 0.941 ± 0.012 accuracy on UAV classification at eight principal components vs. 0.880 ± 0.029 for classical SVC. Fall detection showed similar performance with minor quantum-kernel improvement at higher dimensions. Gaussian-noise robustness study showed limited degradation.
AI.conclusion: Digital twins serve as useful, controlled environments for radar quantum machine learning benchmarking prior to measured-data validation and hardware execution.

title: Detectability Limits for Intra-Block Temporal Drift in Finite-Key Entanglement-Based QKD
summary: We study the statistical detectability of intra-block temporal drift in finite-key entanglement-based quantum key distribution, with particular relevance to E91-type parameter estimation and monitoring. Drift is modeled as a mean-preserving Lipschitz perturbation of Bernoulli observables, capturing structured temporal variation that is invisible to global-average tests. For a block of size $n$ and confidence levels $(α,β)$, we formulate a minimax hypothesis-testing problem and define the minimal detectable amplitude. We derive matching lower and upper bounds yielding $δ_{\min}(n,α,β)=Θ(n^{-1/2})$: if $nδ^2 \to 0$, no level-$α$ procedure can guarantee nontrivial uniform power over the admissible drift class, whereas a calibrated CUSUM statistic detects drift at the matching scale. Explicit constants for linear, sinusoidal, and step profiles, together with simulations, confirm the predicted scaling collapse. The result quantifies a finite-block monitoring-resolution limit and is distinct from composable security certification.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes that the minimal detectable amplitude of intra-block temporal drift in entanglement-based QKD scales as Θ(n^{-1/2}), deriving matching lower and upper bounds via minimax hypothesis testing and a calibrated CUSUM statistic, with explicit constants for linear, sinusoidal, and step drift profiles.
AI.motivation: To quantify the fundamental statistical detectability limit of temporal drift within finite key blocks in entanglement-based QKD (E91-type), where structured temporal variation escapes global-average tests and threatens parameter estimation.
AI.method: Formulates a minimax hypothesis-testing problem for mean-preserving Lipschitz perturbations of Bernoulli observables; derives lower bounds via information-theoretic arguments and upper bounds via a calibrated CUSUM change-point detection statistic.
AI.result: Minimal detectable drift amplitude δ_min(n,α,β) = Θ(n^{-1/2}); if nδ²→0 no level-α procedure has uniform power over the drift class; the CUSUM statistic achieves detection at this matching scale. Explicit constants are provided for linear, sinusoidal, and step drift profiles, with simulations confirming scaling collapse.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a finite-block monitoring-resolution limit for temporal drift detection in QKD parameter estimation, distinct from composable security certification, and provides a practical benchmark for drift-aware protocol design.

title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Machine Learning Algorithms for Multi-Output Time-Series Forecasting at Utility Scale
summary: Multi-output time-series forecasting in energy systems is challenging because of nonlinear dynamics, multi-scale seasonality, and strong dependencies across correlated series. In this work, we investigate two hybrid quantum-classical frameworks for multi-stream time-series forecasting on a real Smart Meter dataset comprising 103 household electricity consumption time-series, with experiments executed on the $ibm\_marrakesh$ superconducting quantum processor. The first model, Kernelized Quantum Reservoir Computing with Repeated Measurement (KQRC-RM), combines coupled quantum reservoirs, ancilla-assisted repeated measurement, and kernelized readouts to model temporal dynamics and cross-stream correlations jointly. For a 3-stream time-series input and output, the KQRC-RM model using 114 qubits achieves an MAE of 0.0811 on MPS simulator (36.92\% improvement over its classical analog) whereas performance degrades to an MAE of 0.1524 on hardware. The second, a Projected Quantum Kernel Gaussian Process (QGP), replaces fidelity-based kernels with projected kernels constructed from local reduced-state statistics. Using a topology-aware 100-qubit QGP model to predict 100 multi-output time-series values, we observe 49\% of time-series outputs achieve high-accuracy predictions (MAE $<0.15$), with an average MAE of $0.082$ for this low-error group. The medium-error regime (MAE $0.15$-$0.35$) has an average MAE of $0.229$, while the high-error regime (MAE $>0.35$) has an average MAE of $0.664$. Overall, this reduces the average MAE relative to the classical GP baseline by 62.01\% on MPS simulator and 40.37\% on hardware. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of hybrid quantum machine learning for multi-input, multi-output time-series forecasting at the 100+ qubit scale on NISQ devices.

AI.tldr: Two hybrid quantum-classical frameworks (KQRC-RM and QGP) are proposed for multi-stream time-series forecasting on a real Smart Meter dataset. KQRC-RM achieved 36.92% MAE improvement (simulator) but degraded on hardware; QGP achieved 62.01% MAE improvement on simulator and 40.37% on hardware over classical GP, demonstrating feasibility of hybrid quantum ML at 100+ qubit scale on NISQ devices.
AI.motivation: Multi-output time-series forecasting in energy systems is challenging due to nonlinear dynamics, multi-scale seasonality, and strong cross-stream dependencies, motivating the exploration of hybrid quantum-classical approaches to overcome limitations of classical models.
AI.method: Two models are proposed: (1) Kernelized Quantum Reservoir Computing with Repeated Measurement (KQRC-RM), combining coupled quantum reservoirs, ancilla-assisted repeated measurement, and kernelized readouts; (2) Projected Quantum Kernel Gaussian Process (QGP), replacing fidelity-based kernels with projected kernels from local reduced-state statistics. Experiments are conducted on a 103-household Smart Meter dataset using the ibm_marrakesh superconducting processor.
AI.result: KQRC-RM (114 qubits, 3-stream): MAE 0.0811 on simulator (36.92% improvement over classical), 0.1524 on hardware. QGP (100 qubits, 100-stream): 49% outputs achieve high accuracy (MAE<0.15, avg 0.082), medium-error avg MAE 0.229, high-error avg MAE 0.664; 62.01% improvement on simulator and 40.37% on hardware over classical GP baseline.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid quantum-classical machine learning is feasible for multi-input, multi-output time-series forecasting at the 100+ qubit scale on NISQ devices, with QGP demonstrating better hardware robustness than KQRC-RM.

title: Quantum non-demolition measurements as a practical primitive for fault-tolerant computation against biased noise
summary: Leveraging noise bias, where phase-flip errors dominate over bit-flips, can drastically reduce the hardware overhead of fault-tolerant quantum computation, but existing approaches require bias-preserving CNOT gates whose implementation remains experimentally challenging and is provably impossible for strictly two-dimensional systems. We show that high-fidelity quantum non-demolition (QND) multi-qubit Pauli $Z$ measurements provide an equally powerful yet more accessible primitive. We demonstrate that such measurements can fully replace bias-preserving CNOT gates for compiling all operations required by bias-tailored error correction, including stabilizer measurements for repetition codes, XZZX surface codes, and LDPC codes. We propose concrete physical implementations of this primitive for two platforms: solid-state nuclear spins coupled to electron spin ancillas, and dissipatively stabilized superconducting cat qubits. Through circuit-level numerical simulations, we show that an asymmetric XZZX surface code implemented with weight-four QND $Z$ measurements achieves a phase-flip threshold of $\sim\!1.25\%$ and provides a qubit overhead reduction of up to $6\times$ compared to a bias-unaware surface code at noise bias $η= 10^4$. In the regime of very large bias, a repetition code with QND $Z$ measurements attains a threshold of $\sim\!2.3\%$ and achieves overhead comparable to that of a bias-preserving CNOT scheme, without requiring such a gate. Our results establish QND multi-$Z$ measurements as a practical and hardware-efficient route to fault-tolerant quantum computation for a broad class of biased-noise platforms.

AI.tldr: High-fidelity QND multi-qubit Pauli Z measurements can replace bias-preserving CNOT gates for fault-tolerant quantum computation under biased noise, achieving comparable or better thresholds and up to 6× qubit overhead reduction without requiring the experimentally challenging CNOT gates.
AI.motivation: Leveraging noise bias (phase-flip errors dominating over bit-flips) reduces hardware overhead for fault-tolerant quantum computation, but existing approaches rely on bias-preserving CNOT gates, which are experimentally challenging and provably impossible in strictly 2D systems. The authors seek a more accessible primitive.
AI.method: The authors propose using high-fidelity QND multi-qubit Pauli Z measurements to replace bias-preserving CNOT gates. They show this primitive can compile all operations for bias-tailored error correction (repetition codes, XZZX surface codes, LDPC codes). They propose physical implementations for solid-state nuclear spins coupled to electron spin ancillas and dissipatively stabilized superconducting cat qubits, and perform circuit-level numerical simulations.
AI.result: Asymmetric XZZX surface code with weight-four QND Z measurements achieves a phase-flip threshold of ~1.25% and up to 6× qubit overhead reduction compared to bias-unaware surface code at noise bias η=10^4. Repetition code with QND Z measurements attains a threshold of ~2.3% at very large bias, with overhead comparable to bias-preserving CNOT schemes.
AI.conclusion: QND multi-Z measurements provide a practical, hardware-efficient route to fault-tolerant quantum computation for biased-noise platforms, eliminating the need for bias-preserving CNOT gates while achieving comparable performance.

title: A Matched Spectral Benchmark of Quantum Inspired Feature Maps
summary: Quantum machine learning is often motivated by the idea that quantum systems can expose useful high-dimensional structure that is difficult to access with classical models. We isolate one central component of this claim: the fixed data-encoding map. Amplitude, angle, and basis encoding are evaluated as deterministic feature maps for classical supervised learning under matched output dimensionality and strong classical controls. The benchmark compares these encodings against raw linear models, random Fourier features, polynomial features, PCA, RBF SVMs, and shallow neural networks across diverse classical datasets. Rather than treating performance as a single endpoint, we analyze the geometry of each representation through effective rank, condition number, centered kernel alignment, predictive performance, and practical overhead. The resulting picture is mechanistic: amplitude encoding can remove magnitude information through unit-sphere normalization, angle encoding can become geometrically redundant with raw linear features, and basis encoding can impose a binary Hamming geometry that is poorly aligned with smooth decision structure. These findings do not argue against quantum computation, however, they show that fixed quantum-inspired encoding geometry alone is not a reliable source of machine-learning advantage on classical data.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates three fixed quantum data-encoding maps (amplitude, angle, basis) as classical feature maps, finding that their geometric properties—unit-sphere normalization, linear redundancy, or Hamming geometry—do not provide intrinsic advantages over classical methods for supervised learning on classical data.
AI.motivation: To isolate and test the claim that quantum systems can expose useful high-dimensional structure inaccessible to classical models, specifically by examining the fixed data-encoding map as a central component of this claim.
AI.method: Benchmark amplitude, angle, and basis encodings as deterministic feature maps against raw linear models, random Fourier features, polynomial features, PCA, RBF SVMs, and shallow neural networks across diverse classical datasets. Analyze geometry via effective rank, condition number, centered kernel alignment, predictive performance, and practical overhead.
AI.result: Amplitude encoding removes magnitude information via unit-sphere normalization; angle encoding becomes geometrically redundant with raw linear features; basis encoding imposes a binary Hamming geometry misaligned with smooth decision structure. Fixed quantum-inspired encoding geometry alone is not a reliable source of ML advantage on classical data.
AI.conclusion: The findings do not argue against quantum computation, but show that fixed quantum-inspired encoding geometry is not inherently advantageous for classical data machine learning tasks.

title: Local Impurity Induced Growth and Scrambling in Clean Free Fermions
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures; Supplemental Material: 17 pages, 9 figures
summary: We study impurity-induced particle growth and scrambling in clean one-dimensional free-fermion systems. We show that a single local impurity can act as a branching source: particle or operator weight propagates coherently into the free bulk, returns to the impurity, and is locally converted into additional degrees of freedom. We develop this branching picture in three complementary settings: a monitored free-fermion model with feedback, a fully unitary interacting particle model, and Heisenberg operator dynamics with an interacting impurity. In the monitored model, we find a feedback-driven transition for both boundary and bulk impurities. In the unitary particle and operator models, a boundary impurity gives rise to an analogous transition from saturation to sustained growth and scrambling. These results reveal how a single impurity can generate complex many-body dynamics in an otherwise clean and free quantum system.

AI.tldr: A single local impurity in clean 1D free-fermion systems can act as a branching source, driving particle/operator growth and scrambling, leading to phase transitions in monitored, unitary particle, and operator dynamics settings.
AI.motivation: To understand how a single impurity can generate complex many-body dynamics and scrambling in an otherwise clean and free quantum system.
AI.method: The authors study three complementary models: (1) a monitored free-fermion model with feedback, (2) a fully unitary interacting particle model, and (3) Heisenberg operator dynamics with an interacting impurity.
AI.result: A single local impurity acts as a branching source, causing coherent propagation and local conversion of particle/operator weight. A feedback-driven transition is found in the monitored model for both boundary and bulk impurities. Boundary impurities in unitary particle and operator models show an analogous transition from saturation to sustained growth and scrambling.
AI.conclusion: A single impurity can drive complex many-body dynamics—including transitions to sustained growth and scrambling—in otherwise clean and free quantum systems.

title: Multiple fidelities and joint numerical range
comment: 17 pages, 1 figure, submitted to JPA, comments are welcome
summary: We investigate the effectiveness of entanglement detection based on multiple fidelities via the geometry of the joint separable numerical range. When all reference states are product states, we derive a necessary and sufficient criterion for such detection: either some pair of reference states has nontrivial moduli of the local inner products on both subsystems, or the orthogonal complement of the span of the reference states is completely entangled. We further show that there exist sets of reference product states for which no proper subset is effective for entanglement detection, whereas the full set is. A typical example of this phenomenon is provided by unextendible product bases. Moreover, for a pair of reference product states on a bipartite system with arbitrary local dimensions, we characterize both the joint numerical range and the joint separable numerical range, showing that the joint separable numerical range is determined solely by their local fidelities, as illustrated by a representative two-qubit example. Our results offer a systematic approach to designing effective entanglement witnesses and lay the groundwork for extensions to higher-dimensional and multipartite scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper studies entanglement detection using multiple fidelities through the geometry of joint separable numerical range, deriving criteria for product-state reference sets and characterizing ranges for pairs of reference states.
AI.motivation: To develop a systematic framework for designing effective entanglement witnesses based on multiple fidelity measurements, leveraging geometric properties of the joint separable numerical range.
AI.method: The authors use geometric analysis of the joint separable numerical range. For sets of product reference states, they derive necessary and sufficient criteria for entanglement detection. They analyze unextendible product bases as examples, and characterize joint numerical ranges for pairs of reference states in bipartite systems.
AI.result: A necessary and sufficient criterion: either some pair of reference states has nontrivial moduli of local inner products on both subsystems, or the orthogonal complement of the span of reference states is completely entangled. There exist sets where no proper subset suffices but the full set does (e.g., unextendible product bases). For a pair of reference product states, the joint separable numerical range is determined solely by local fidelities.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a systematic approach to designing entanglement witnesses and lays foundations for extensions to higher-dimensional and multipartite systems.

title: Semiclassical Propagation and the Dynamics of Configuration Space
summary: This work explores the non-relativistic quantum propagator $K(x,t)$ as a solution of the Schrödinger equation. We suppose that the propagator takes the form ${\rm exp}\left(\frac{\mathrm{i}}{\hbar}S+R\right)$, generalizing the usual WKB ansatz by allowing an additive exponent $R$ whose role as a measure of quantumness is investigated. Since $S$ is subject to the assumption that it is a solution of the Hamilton-Jacobi equation, here we are further interested in the role of $R$ and its interpretation as a measure of quantumness. Several systems are studied as concrete examples to illustrate this approach. Furthermore, a proposal to generalize it for fields is put forward. This is tested for some simple systems. Finally, the possibilities to use this approach for the case of systems whose dynamics are controlled by the Hamiltonian constraint are analyzed.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates a generalized WKB ansatz for the non-relativistic quantum propagator, adding an exponent R to the usual semiclassical action S (Hamilton-Jacobi solution). R is interpreted as a measure of quantumness. The approach is tested on several systems, extended to field theory, and analyzed for Hamiltonian-constrained systems.
AI.motivation: To generalize the standard WKB propagator by introducing an additive exponent R that quantifies deviations from classical behavior, providing a clearer measure of quantumness beyond the semiclassical approximation.
AI.method: The propagator is expressed as exp(iS/ℏ + R), where S satisfies the Hamilton-Jacobi equation. R is studied as a quantum correction term. The approach is demonstrated on concrete non-relativistic systems, extended to field theories, and analyzed under Hamiltonian constraints.
AI.result: The ansatz successfully characterizes quantumness via R in several systems. The field-theoretic generalization is tested on simple systems. The method shows applicability to constrained Hamiltonian dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The R exponent provides a useful measure of quantumness in the propagator formalism, and the approach can be generalized to field theory and Hamiltonian-constrained systems.

title: Fermi-Dirac machines as quantizations of neurons
summary: Fermi-Dirac machines were proposed recently as an approach to solving semidefinite optimization problems on quantum computers. Here, we reinterpret them as canonical quantizations of classical neurons. By viewing a classical neuron as an activation function applied to a parameterized classical Hamiltonian, we quantize this model by replacing classical variables with operators whose eigenvalues encode their possible values. This follows the standard approach to canonical quantization in quantum mechanics. Crucially, when the Hamiltonian consists of commuting operators, our construction reduces exactly to a classical neuron. More generally, our approach yields an activation observable, defined as an activation function applied to a parameterized quantum Hamiltonian. The output of this quantized neuron is a random variable with expectation value equal to that of the activation observable with respect to an input state. We develop efficient hybrid quantum-classical algorithms for evaluating outputs and gradients of our quantized neurons, enabling evaluation and training. These algorithms rely on basic primitives that include random sampling, Hamiltonian simulation, and the Hadamard test. We also quantize a whole host of other activation functions, including the smooth rectified linear unit (ReLU), sigmoid linear unit, Gaussian-smoothed ReLU, and Gaussian error linear unit (GeLU), which are known to be useful for deep learning applications. Numerical experiments indicate that neurons based on quantum Hamiltonians can learn functions that classical neurons cannot. We further define a computational decision problem based on Fermi-Dirac neurons and prove that it is BQP-complete, providing complexity-theoretic evidence against efficient classical simulation. Finally, we generalize our approach to continuous quantum variables and sketch two different ways of composing these neurons into networks.

AI.tldr: The paper reinterprets Fermi-Dirac machines as canonical quantizations of classical neurons, replacing classical variables with quantum operators. It defines activation observables, develops hybrid quantum-classical algorithms for evaluation and training, and shows that quantum neurons can learn functions classical neurons cannot. A BQP-completeness result provides evidence against efficient classical simulation.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between quantum computing and neural network architectures by providing a principled quantization framework for classical neurons, enabling the construction of quantum neural networks that can learn beyond classical capabilities.
AI.method: The authors apply canonical quantization (replacing classical variables with operators) to classical neuron models. They define activation observables as activation functions applied to parameterized quantum Hamiltonians, and develop hybrid quantum-classical algorithms using random sampling, Hamiltonian simulation, and the Hadamard test for computing outputs and gradients. They also define a BQP-complete decision problem based on Fermi-Dirac neurons.
AI.result: The quantization framework reduces exactly to classical neurons when the Hamiltonian consists of commuting operators. Numerical experiments show that quantum Hamiltonians-based neurons can learn functions that classical neurons cannot. The associated decision problem is proven BQP-complete, suggesting these quantum neurons are unlikely to be efficiently simulable classically.
AI.conclusion: The canonical quantization approach provides a principled way to construct quantum neural networks with provable advantages over classical counterparts, supported by both empirical evidence and complexity-theoretic guarantees.

title: Distinguishing Bohmian contextuality from Kochen-Specker contextuality
summary: Quantum contextuality is a concept used to describe the property of hidden-variable theory that measurement outcomes predetermined by the hidden variables depend on the measurement context. The term measurement context can have different meanings, giving rise to different flavours of quantum contextuality. The first discovered flavour is Kochen-Specker (KS) contextuality where measurement outcomes will depend on what compatible measurements are jointly performed with the selected measurement. Another flavour, here to be compared with KS contextuality, is that referred to in Bohmian mechanics where outcomes of some specific measurements are not completely specified by the model state, but depend also on specifics of the measurement device used. It has been claimed that this type of Bohmian contextuality is necessary to enable KS contextuality in a hidden variable model. In this paper we show that this is not the case. The recently proposed Contextual Ontological Model (COM) [Hindlycke and Larsson, Phys. Rev. Lett. 2022] produces KS contextual predictions but does not have the Bohmian contextuality; the outcome of every measurement allowed by COM can be predicted from the model state itself. This distinguishes Bohmian contextuality from KS contextuality, and enables individual study of the two concepts.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that Bohmian contextuality is not necessary for Kochen-Specker (KS) contextuality, using the Contextual Ontological Model (COM) which produces KS contextual predictions without Bohmian contextuality, allowing separate study of the two concepts.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether Bohmian contextuality is a necessary condition for Kochen-Specker contextuality in hidden-variable theories, and to distinguish the two flavors of quantum contextuality for independent analysis.
AI.method: The authors analyze the Contextual Ontological Model (COM) recently proposed by Hindlycke and Larsson, examining whether it exhibits Bohmian contextuality (where measurement outcomes depend on device specifics beyond the model state) while producing KS contextual predictions.
AI.result: The COM produces KS contextual predictions but does not exhibit Bohmian contextuality; every measurement outcome in COM is fully determined by the model state itself, without dependence on measurement device specifics.
AI.conclusion: Bohmian contextuality is not necessary for KS contextuality, distinguishing the two concepts and enabling their individual study.

title: Quantum Dynamics of Interacting dissipative oscillators: A novel scheme
summary: We investigate the dynamics of interacting quantum harmonic oscillators coupled to thermal reservoirs under the influence of an external driving field. In a novel theoretical scheme, we first analyze the case of two interacting oscillators, each coupled to its own thermal reservoir, with an external source applied to the first oscillator. By diagonalizing the total Hamiltonian through successive Bogoliubov transformations, we obtain explicit expressions for the oscillator energies. A key finding is that off resonance, the energy of the second oscillator grows unboundedly, whereas on resonance, it remains bounded and periodic. We then derive the Husimi functions for both oscillators and the reduced Husimi functions for initially separable coherent and number states. The shift of the Husimi function's maximum away from the origin at zero temperature confirms continuous energy gain under specific parameter conditions. An explicit formula for the reduced density matrix components in the number state basis is also provided. Finally, we generalize the model to $n$ interacting oscillators in a thermal medium driven by a classical field. For the three-oscillator case, we show that on resonance, the energies of the first and third oscillators grow, while the energy of the second oscillator remains periodically bounded. These results offer insights into energy transfer and localization in coupled oscillator systems in thermal environments.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the dynamics of coupled quantum harmonic oscillators in thermal reservoirs under external driving, finding that off-resonance the second oscillator's energy grows unboundedly, while on resonance it remains bounded and periodic. The model is generalized to n oscillators, with specific results for three oscillators showing selective energy localization.
AI.motivation: To understand energy transfer and localization in coupled quantum oscillator systems interacting with thermal environments under external driving, particularly the conditions leading to unbounded vs. bounded energy growth.
AI.method: The Hamiltonian is diagonalized via successive Bogoliubov transformations. Husimi functions and reduced density matrix components are derived for initially separable coherent and number states. The model is generalized to n interacting oscillators.
AI.result: Off-resonance, the second oscillator's energy grows unboundedly; on resonance, it remains bounded and periodic. For three oscillators, on resonance the first and third oscillators grow in energy while the second remains periodically bounded. The Husimi function's maximum shifts away from the origin at zero temperature, confirming continuous energy gain.
AI.conclusion: The results offer insights into energy transfer and localization in coupled oscillator systems in thermal environments, demonstrating resonance-based control of energy flow.

title: Quantum Otto machine with $q$-deformed Pöschl-Teller oscillator
summary: We study the impact of the potential parameters of the q-deformed modified Pöschl-Teller potential on the thermodynamic performance of a quantum Otto cycle, where the $q$-deformed modified Pöschl-Teller potential serves as the working substance. Analytical expressions for the energy spectrum and wave functions are derived, enabling a systematic investigation of heat exchange, work output, efficiency, and coefficient of performance. We show that $q$-deformation modifies the energy spectrum and creates distinct performance regions in the ($q$, $Δ$) parameter space. Low ($Δ$) and high ($q$) favour optimal heat engine efficiency, whereas high ($Δ$) and low ($q$) improve refrigerator performance. The heat engine efficiency peaks in the low-($Δ$), high-($q$) regime. These results highlight the q-deformed modified Pöschl-Teller potential as a versatile and tunable platform for exploring potential parameter-driven effects in quantum thermal machines.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how the parameters (q and Δ) of a q-deformed modified Pöschl-Teller potential affect the thermodynamic performance of a quantum Otto cycle, finding that low Δ and high q optimize heat engine efficiency, while high Δ and low q improve refrigerator performance.
AI.motivation: To understand how the potential parameters of the q-deformed modified Pöschl-Teller potential influence the thermodynamic performance of a quantum Otto cycle, and to explore its tunability as a working substance in quantum thermal machines.
AI.method: Analytical derivations of energy spectrum and wave functions for the q-deformed modified Pöschl-Teller potential, followed by systematic thermodynamic analysis of heat exchange, work output, efficiency, and coefficient of performance in a quantum Otto cycle.
AI.result: q-deformation modifies the energy spectrum, creating distinct performance regions: low Δ and high q favor optimal heat engine efficiency, while high Δ and low q enhance refrigerator performance.
AI.conclusion: The q-deformed modified Pöschl-Teller potential is a versatile and tunable platform for parameter-driven effects in quantum thermal machines.

title: Electrodynamics as a Theory of Persistent Stochastic Processes
summary:
A process-theoretic approach to electrodynamics based on persistent Kac-type stochastic processes is developed. Finite-velocity stochastic propagation is taken as primary, while relativistic wave equations arise as emergent descriptions after analytic continuation of Telegrapher-type dynamics. The Dirac and Maxwell equations are interpreted as arising from closely related persistent propagation structures differing only in spin representation.
  The framework is not intended to modify the successful empirical predictions of quantum electrodynamics, but to provide a different underlying ontology.
