Experimental results show that the three complementary probes proposed in this work, namely the distance to Porter-Thomas statistics, Shannon entropy, and Out-of-Time-Ordered-Correlator-equivalent observables, exhibit close agreement with theoretical predictions and consistently distinguish chaotic and integrable dynamics. Our work provides a scalable route for investigating complex quantum dynamics on programmable photonic platforms while leveraging the intrinsic advantages of boson sampling through multiphoton interference and complex output statistics.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes Fock-state boson sampling as a probe of quantum chaos using a programmable silicon quantum photonic chip, demonstrating three complementary chaos diagnostics (Porter-Thomas distance, Shannon entropy, OTOC-equivalent observables) that distinguish chaotic from integrable dynamics, marking the first integrated-photonic demonstration of quantum-chaos probes via boson sampling.
AI.motivation: Quantum chaos is crucial for understanding complex quantum dynamics, but probing it on integrated photonic platforms remains unexplored due to the lack of a clear connection between programmable photonic dynamics and established chaos diagnostics.
AI.method: The authors establish Fock-state boson sampling as a practical probe of quantum chaos by exploiting the sensitivity of multiphoton interference to random-matrix properties of single-particle unitary dynamics, and implement this framework on a programmable silicon quantum photonic chip.
AI.result: Three complementary probes—distance to Porter-Thomas statistics, Shannon entropy, and OTOC-equivalent observables—exhibit close agreement with theoretical predictions and consistently distinguish chaotic and integrable dynamics on the integrated photonic platform.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a scalable route for investigating complex quantum dynamics on programmable photonic platforms, leveraging the intrinsic advantages of boson sampling through multiphoton interference and complex output statistics.

title: Strategic Non-Shareability of Quantum Correlations
summary: Correlations distributed by a mediator are usually valued for the coordination they enable between authorized agents, but in adversarial settings a more decisive property is whether the same coordination can be inherited by an outside colluder without disturbing the authorized marginal. Classical shared randomness is freely copyable, so a hidden seed coordinating two agents can be duplicated for a third; entanglement is constrained by monogamy, which can forbid such lossless extensions in strongly nonlocal regimes. We turn this asymmetry into an operational resource for private-information games. For a fixed authorized behavior $P_{12}$, we define its \emph{collusive shadow} as the set of relabelled behaviors a colluder can reproduce in any admissible tripartite extension preserving $P_{12}$, and we identify \emph{strategic non-shareability} with the distance from this shadow. We prove that, on finite alphabets, the game-optimized anti-collusion capacity equals the total-variation distance to the shadow; a fixed game provides a task-specific separating witness, while optimization over relabelled games recovers the full distance. In the CHSH score slice, Toner--Verstraete monogamy yields the exact certified frontier, so the Bell local bound $S_{12}=2$ is the sharp onset of positive certified anti-collusion power, saturating at $1/(2\sqrt{2})$ for the maximally entangled CHSH strategy. Classical hidden-variable mediators have zero capacity in this slice. We complement these results with two operational tools: a Hoeffding-based finite-data certification protocol that turns observed Bell scores into confidence-bounded anti-collusion certificates, and a level-2 NPA semidefinite relaxation that extends certified upper envelopes to tilted Bell inequalities. These results recast entanglement monogamy as a measurable shareability deficit for quantum-mediated strategic networks.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes the non-shareability of quantum correlations—enforced by entanglement monogamy—as an operational resource for private-information games. The authors define a "collusive shadow" for a bipartite behavior and prove that anti-collusion capacity equals total-variation distance to this shadow. They show that CHSH Bell violation beyond the local bound yields positive certified anti-collusion power, provide a finite-data certification protocol, and extend analysis via NPA relaxations to tilted Bell inequalities.
AI.motivation: To leverage the asymmetry between classical shared randomness (freely copyable) and quantum entanglement (monogamous) as an operational resource for preventing collusion in adversarial settings, by quantifying and certifying the strategic non-shareability of quantum correlations.
AI.method: Defines the "collusive shadow" of an authorized bipartite behavior as the set of behaviors a colluder can reproduce in any tripartite extension preserving the marginals. Proves that game-optimized anti-collusion capacity equals total-variation distance to this shadow. Uses CHSH score slice with Toner–Verstraete monogamy for exact frontier. Develops a Hoeffding-based finite-data certification protocol and a level-2 NPA SDP relaxation for tilted Bell inequalities.
AI.result: The Bell local bound S=2 is the sharp onset of positive certified anti-collusion power, saturating at 1/(2√2) for maximally entangled CHSH strategy. Classical hidden-variable mediators have zero capacity in this slice.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement monogamy can be operationally recast as a measurable shareability deficit for quantum-mediated strategic networks, providing a resource for anti-collusion certification.

title: Beyond Logical Circuits: Hardware-Aware Analysis of Expressibility and Trainability in Variational Quantum Algorithms
summary: Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) rely on parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs), whose performance is governed by expressibility and trainability. Existing studies typically evaluate these properties at the logical circuit level, implicitly assuming that designed PQCs remain unchanged during hardware execution. In practice, however, hardware-aware transpilation modifies circuit structure through qubit mapping, routing, and basis decomposition, potentially altering PQC behavior. In this paper, we perform a systematic hardware-aware analysis of expressibility and trainability by comparing logical and transpiled PQCs across multiple ansatz families, qubit counts, and circuit depths. Expressibility is measured using fidelity-based KL divergence, while trainability is quantified through gradient variance. Our results show that transpilation acts as an implicit architectural perturbation, producing strongly ansatz-dependent effects. Expressibility deviations exceed upto 125% in some cases, while trainability variations reach up to 25%. Structured ansatzes are generally more robust, whereas highly entangled architectures are more sensitive to transpilation-induced transformations. We further show that transpilation can alter the commonly assumed expressibility-trainability trade-off, demonstrating that logical-level analyses may not reliably predict hardware-level behavior. These findings highlight the importance of hardware-aware evaluation for accurate characterization of VQAs.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that hardware-aware transpilation significantly alters the expressibility (up to 125% deviation) and trainability (up to 25% deviation) of parameterized quantum circuits in variational quantum algorithms, challenging the validity of logical-level analyses for predicting real hardware performance.
AI.motivation: Existing studies evaluate PQC expressibility and trainability at the logical circuit level, implicitly assuming designed circuits remain unchanged during hardware execution. However, hardware-aware transpilation modifies circuit structure through qubit mapping, routing, and basis decomposition, potentially altering PQC behavior, motivating the need for systematic hardware-aware analysis.
AI.method: The authors systematically compare logical and transpiled PQCs across multiple ansatz families, qubit counts, and circuit depths. Expressibility is measured using fidelity-based KL divergence, while trainability is quantified through gradient variance.
AI.result: Transpilation acts as an implicit architectural perturbation with ansatz-dependent effects: expressibility deviations exceed 125% in some cases, trainability variations reach 25%. Structured ansatzes are more robust, while highly entangled architectures are more sensitive. Transpilation can alter the expressibility-trainability trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Logical-level analyses may not reliably predict hardware-level behavior; hardware-aware evaluation is essential for accurate characterization of VQAs.

title: High fidelity preservation of photonic hyperentanglement in a free-space optical delay line
summary: Photonic hyperentanglement enables increased information capacity and enhanced functionality for quantum communication and networking. However, synchronization of hyperentangled photon pairs requires maintaining correlations simultaneously across multiple degrees of freedom (DOFs). The preservation of polarization and energy-time entanglement in hyperentangled photon pairs is demonstrated using a free-space optical delay line based on nested Herriott cells. After a delay of 647 ns, a two-photon interference visibility of 93.9(3)% is observed in the energy-time DOF, while a CHSH parameter of 2.758(5) is obtained in the polarization DOF. These results confirm that entanglement correlations in both DOFs are preserved after propagation through the delay line. They demonstrate that free-space optical delay lines are compatible with complex photonic quantum states and provide a promising route toward delay-based memories for synchronization and multiplexing in quantum networks.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates the preservation of both polarization and energy-time entanglement in hyperentangled photon pairs after a 647 ns delay through a free-space optical delay line based on nested Herriott cells, achieving high visibility (93.9%) and CHSH parameter (2.758), showing compatibility with complex quantum states for quantum network synchronization.
AI.motivation: Photonic hyperentanglement can increase information capacity and enhance functionality for quantum communication and networking, but synchronization of hyperentangled photon pairs requires maintaining correlations simultaneously across multiple degrees of freedom (DOFs).
AI.method: A free-space optical delay line based on nested Herriott cells was used to delay hyperentangled photon pairs. Two-photon interference visibility was measured in the energy-time DOF, and the CHSH parameter was measured in the polarization DOF after a 647 ns delay.
AI.result: After a 647 ns delay, two-photon interference visibility of 93.9(3)% was observed in the energy-time DOF, and a CHSH parameter of 2.758(5) was obtained in the polarization DOF.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement correlations in both DOFs are preserved after propagation through the delay line, demonstrating that free-space optical delay lines are compatible with complex photonic quantum states and offer a promising route toward delay-based memories for synchronization and multiplexing in quantum networks.

title: Dissipative Time Quasicrystals from Multilevel Interference
summary: Boundary time crystals exhibit spontaneous breaking of continuous time-translation symmetry through persistent periodic oscillations in driven-dissipative many-body systems. Here, we show that multilevel interference provides a natural route beyond periodic order, enabling dissipative time quasicrystals without externally imposed quasiperiodic driving. We consider a collectively driven-dissipative four-level ensemble with two degenerate excited states and two degenerate ground states. In the thermodynamic limit, the exact mean-field dynamics reduces to an irrational flow on a two-dimensional torus, yielding quasiperiodic order parameters with discrete spectra generated by two incommensurate fundamental frequencies. Vanishing maximal Lyapunov exponents demonstrate that the nonlinear self-consistent dynamics remains nonchaotic. Our results establish a minimal interference-induced mechanism for time-quasiperiodic order and open a route toward higher-dimensional quasiperiodic dynamics in multilevel systems.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that multilevel quantum interference in a driven-dissipative four-level atomic ensemble naturally produces time quasicrystals—quasiperiodic oscillations with two incommensurate frequencies—without external quasiperiodic driving, establishing a minimal mechanism for time-quasiperiodic order.
AI.motivation: To extend beyond conventional boundary time crystals (which exhibit periodic time-translation symmetry breaking) and realize dissipative time quasicrystals without needing externally imposed quasiperiodic driving.
AI.method: A collectively driven-dissipative four-level ensemble with two degenerate excited states and two degenerate ground states is analyzed using exact mean-field dynamics in the thermodynamic limit, with Lyapunov exponents to characterize chaos.
AI.result: The dynamics reduce to an irrational flow on a 2D torus, yielding quasiperiodic order parameters with discrete spectra from two incommensurate fundamental frequencies, and vanishing maximal Lyapunov exponents confirm nonchaotic behavior.
AI.conclusion: Multilevel interference offers a natural, minimal route to time-quasiperiodic order and opens pathways toward higher-dimensional quasiperiodic dynamics in multilevel systems.

title: Homomorphic Quantum Error Correction
summary: Homomorphic quantum error correction aims to protect quantum data against both unauthorized access and environmental noise during server-based processing. We investigate the algebraic compatibility between quantum homomorphic encryption and quantum error correction, determining precise conditions under which encrypted encoded states remain inside the relevant code space during storage and computation. Our work establishes a necessary and sufficient criterion for an $[[n,1,d]]$ stabilizer code to remain compatible with the restricted transversal block-Pauli masking $U_{\rm enc}(a,b)=(X^aZ^b)^{\otimes n}$, stated explicitly for $[[n,1,d]]$ codes and extending directly to code-space preservation for $[[n,k,d]]$ codes. We verify this condition for standard examples (bit-flip and Shor codes, with the phase-flip repetition code following analogously), derive a practical criterion for Calderbank-Shor-Steane codes, and extend the analysis to three-dimensional color codes. A critical challenge emerges for non-Clifford gate implementation: the Shor code lacks a naive transversal $T$-gate implementation of the desired logical operation on encrypted encoded data. We present two routes around this obstruction. First, suitable triorthogonal codes admit transversal $T$-type logical implementations, up to Clifford corrections. Second, logical-gate masking gives code-space compatibility for arbitrary stabilizer codes, provided that suitable unitary representatives of the required logical gates are available. These results separate code-space compatibility from a full cryptographic security proof and provide explicit criteria for combining error correction with homomorphic processing in cloud quantum computing.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes necessary and sufficient criteria for stabilizer codes to remain compatible with homomorphic quantum encryption (transversal block-Pauli masking), analyzes specific codes (bit-flip, Shor, CSS, 3D color codes), identifies a non-Clifford obstruction in the Shor code, and proposes two solutions using triorthogonal codes or logical-gate masking.
AI.motivation: To protect quantum data against both unauthorized access and environmental noise during server-based processing by combining homomorphic encryption with quantum error correction.
AI.method: The authors establish a necessary and sufficient criterion for $[[n,1,d]]$ stabilizer codes compatible with transversal block-Pauli masking $U_{\rm enc}(a,b)=(X^aZ^b)^{\otimes n}$, extend to $[[n,k,d]]$ codes, verify on standard codes, derive practical criteria for CSS codes, analyze 3D color codes, and propose solutions for the non-Clifford obstruction via triorthogonal codes and logical-gate masking.
AI.result: A necessary and sufficient compatibility criterion for $[[n,1,d]]$ stabilizer codes is established; verified for bit-flip, Shor, and phase-flip codes; a practical criterion for CSS codes is derived; 3D color codes are analyzed; the Shor code lacks a naive transversal $T$-gate; two solutions (triorthogonal codes with transversal $T$, logical-gate masking for arbitrary codes) are presented.
AI.conclusion: Code-space compatibility is separated from full cryptographic security; explicit criteria for combining error correction with homomorphic processing in cloud quantum computing are provided.

title: Q-LEAK: Quantum-Based LEAKage Verification for Side-Channel Countermeasures
summary: Formal verification of power side-channel leakage and its countermeasures in cryptographic algorithms is challenging, as SAT-based methods fail to scale on XOR-heavy, time-unrolled cryptographic circuits with realistic leakage models. We construct compact Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF) cases modeling one-bit leakage under two-trace conditions, linking key dependence and state evolution. Classical solvers quickly reach complexity limits, so we propose Q-LEAK, a quantum-based verification approach using Grover's algorithm, compiling each CNF into an oracle and applying amplitude amplification to search in O(sqrt(N)) oracle calls, with oracles that encode the two-trace leakage predicate and the CNF constraints. Benchmarking against classical SAT shows both potential gains and practical resource limits. In noiseless tests on 5-7 variable benchmarks, Q-LEAK consistently recovered a satisfying assignment within 1-4 tries, with marked bitstrings amplified clearly above the background distribution, exceeding 20 percent probability. The evaluation of Q-LEAK on real quantum hardware revealed at least one classically verified SAT assignment, despite the presence of noise. These results point to a potential path toward quantum-assisted verification of side-channel protections.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Q-LEAK, a quantum-based verification approach using Grover's algorithm to detect power side-channel leakage in cryptographic circuits, outperforming classical SAT solvers on XOR-heavy, time-unrolled circuits by achieving O(sqrt(N)) search complexity and demonstrating successful assignment recovery in both noiseless simulations and real quantum hardware tests.
AI.motivation: Formal verification of power side-channel leakage and its countermeasures in cryptographic algorithms is challenging because SAT-based methods fail to scale on XOR-heavy, time-unrolled cryptographic circuits with realistic leakage models.
AI.method: Construct compact CNF cases modeling one-bit leakage under two-trace conditions; propose Q-LEAK using Grover's algorithm with amplitude amplification, compiling each CNF into an oracle that encodes the two-trace leakage predicate and CNF constraints, achieving O(sqrt(N)) oracle call complexity.
AI.result: On 5-7 variable benchmarks, Q-LEAK recovered satisfying assignments within 1-4 tries with marked bitstrings exceeding 20% probability. Real quantum hardware tests revealed at least one classically verified SAT assignment despite noise.
AI.conclusion: These results point to a potential path toward quantum-assisted verification of side-channel protections.

title: Wave-particle duality of unpolarized photons
summary: Photons in a two-path interferometer best embody wave-particle duality (WPD), which is a core concept of quantum theory. So far, the WPD relation is commonly written as $V^2+D^2 \leq 1$, where $V$ is the interference fringe visibility and $D$ is path distinguishability, i.e., the distinguishability of which path a photon passed. This inequality is saturated only when the which-way marker (WWM), which embodies which-path information (WPI) via an internal degree of freedom of photons, such as polarization, is in a pure state. For mixed-state WWM, conventionally defined distinguishability underestimates the amount of WPI and thus does not saturate the WPD relation. Here, we introduce a generalized measure of distinguishability $D$ that properly quantifies the WPI and saturates the WPD relation for all pure- and mixed-state WWM within a purification-based framework. To this end, mixed-state WWM is treated as a result of entanglement formation between the WWM and an external degree of freedom, e.g., environment, and $D$ is defined so that it incorporates the total WPI shared between the WWM and the environment. We show that $D$ thus defined is experimentally quantifiable, independently of $V$, without access to the environment. We experimentally evaluate $V$ and $D$ using true single photons generated in the completely mixed (unpolarized) state, and thus verify the saturated WPD relation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a generalized distinguishability measure D that saturates the wave-particle duality relation V² + D² ≤ 1 for both pure and mixed which-way markers, and experimentally verifies it using true single photons in a completely mixed state.
AI.motivation: The conventional WPD relation V² + D² ≤ 1 is only saturated for pure-state which-way markers; for mixed-state WWM, the standard distinguishability underestimates the amount of which-path information, leaving the relation unsaturated.
AI.method: The authors treat mixed-state WWM as resulting from entanglement with an external environment, define a generalized distinguishability D that captures total which-path information shared between WWM and environment, and show D is experimentally measurable without accessing the environment.
AI.result: Experimental verification using true single photons in a completely mixed (unpolarized) state demonstrates that the saturated WPD relation V² + D² = 1 holds for the generalized distinguishability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed generalized distinguishability properly quantifies which-path information for any WWM state and saturates the WPD relation universally, extending the wave-particle duality framework to mixed-state scenarios.

title: QGCL: Quantum-Guided Clause Learning for Cryptanalytic SAT
summary: Power side-channel attacks on AES exploit data-dependent physical leakage to recover secret keys, but turning noisy leakage observations into a verified AES-128 key remains a hard combinational search problem. SAT-assisted power side-channel cryptanalysis addresses this challenge by encoding AES semantics, key constraints, plaintext/ciphertext consistency, and leakage predicates as CNF, so that candidate keys must satisfy the exact cryptographic specification. These cryptanalytic SAT formulas are large and highly structured; our largest controlled AES-oriented power-SCA instances contain up to 39,389 variables and 137,712 clauses, making a full-formula Grover search well beyond the scale studied here and beyond currently practical near-term implementations. We propose QGCL, a Quantum-Guided Conflict-Driven Clause Learning (CDCL) framework in which Grover search is invoked only on small subformulas extracted dynamically around CDCL conflict cores. The quantum subsolver returns candidate assignments and violation scores that bias branching heuristics, while final SAT/UNSAT decisions and key verification remain classical. We evaluate QGCL on AES-oriented cryptanalytic SAT instances derived from power side-channel CNFs with leakage-derived hint configurations, measuring conflicts, restarts, decisions, and propagations. The experiments show consistent reductions in these solver-internal statistics on harder instances, with up to an 86% reduction in conflicts compared with the classical conflict-learning baseline. Parameter sweeps over the number of Grover oracle calls and the subproblem size identify a regime in which a modest quantum resource allocation captures most of the observed improvement.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes QGCL, a hybrid quantum-classical SAT solving framework that uses Grover search on small subformulas extracted from CDCL conflict cores to accelerate power side-channel cryptanalysis of AES, achieving up to 86% reduction in conflicts on hard instances.
AI.motivation: Power side-channel attacks on AES produce noisy leakage observations that must be turned into verified secret keys via a hard combinational search problem. SAT-assisted cryptanalysis encodes this as large, structured CNF formulas (up to ~39K variables, ~137K clauses), but full-formula Grover search is beyond near-term quantum capabilities.
AI.method: QGCL integrates Grover search as a quantum subsolver into classical CDCL: small subformulas are dynamically extracted from conflict cores, the quantum oracle returns candidate assignments and violation scores to bias branching heuristics, while SAT/UNSAT decisions and key verification remain classical.
AI.result: Consistent reductions in solver-internal statistics (conflicts, restarts, decisions, propagations) on harder instances, with up to 86% reduction in conflicts vs. the classical CDCL baseline. Parameter sweeps identify a regime where modest quantum resource allocation captures most of the observed improvement.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid QGCL framework effectively accelerates AES-oriented power-SCA SAT solving with limited quantum resources, demonstrating a practical near-term quantum advantage for structured cryptanalytic problems.

title: Thermalization in Spatially Extended Open Quantum Systems: Local versus Global Markovian Evolution
summary: We investigate the dynamics of a qubit chain locally coupled to a thermal reservoir, modeled through repeated collisions with particles drawn from a heat bath. Under suitable conditions, the resulting Lindblad equation is thermodynamically consistent -- it drives the system toward thermal equilibrium -- while remaining local at short times. This framework reveals a crossover between the global Lindblad equation derived from the secular approximation in weak-coupling theory and the local dissipative models often employed in the literature, which generally fail to ensure thermodynamic consistency.

AI.tldr: The paper studies a qubit chain coupled to a thermal bath via repeated collisions, deriving a Lindblad equation that is both thermodynamically consistent and local at short times. This framework bridges weak-coupling global Lindblad equations and local dissipative models, highlighting a crossover between them.
AI.motivation: To reconcile global Lindblad equations (thermodynamically consistent but derived under secular approximation) with local dissipative models (commonly used but often violate thermodynamic consistency), by introducing a collision-based framework that remains local at short times yet drives the system toward thermal equilibrium.
AI.method: The authors model a qubit chain locally coupled to a thermal reservoir via repeated collisions with heat bath particles. They derive the resulting Lindblad equation and analyze its thermodynamic consistency and locality properties.
AI.result: The framework produces a Lindblad equation that is thermodynamically consistent (drives the system to thermal equilibrium) and local at short times, revealing a crossover between global secular-approximation Lindblad equations and local dissipative models.
AI.conclusion: The collision-based approach provides a unified bridge connecting global and local Lindblad descriptions, offering a thermodynamically consistent yet local dissipative model for open quantum systems.

title: Rethinking Expressibility-Trainability Trade-off in Hybrid Quantum Neural Networks
summary: Hybrid quantum neural networks (HQNNs) integrate parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) within classical networks, where the behavior of the underlying PQCs is often the primary focus of analysis. In this context, expressibility and trainability are widely used to characterize PQC's performance and are commonly assumed to exhibit a trade-off, where highly expressive circuits are more susceptible to barren plateaus. However, the validity of this relationship in HQNNs remains unclear. In this paper, we systematically analyze the expressibility--trainability relationship in HQNNs across varying circuit depths, qubit counts, entanglement topologies. We consider different training configurations, including pure PQCs, quantum-only training in hybrid setting, and full end-to-end training of hybrid models. Our results show that pure PQCs exhibit only a weak and regime-dependent trade-off, while hybrid architectures increasingly disrupt and can eliminate this relationship under full hybrid training. This indicates that classical components reshape the optimization landscape, decoupling trainability from PQC expressibility. We further propose a multi-objective neural architecture search (NAS) framework that jointly optimizes expressibility, trainability, and task performance over a combined classical--quantum design space, revealing different Pareto-optimal solutions under full end-to-end and quantum only training in hybrid setting. different trainability definitions. Our results suggest that hybridization is not just an implementation detail, but a defining factor in the performance of quantum machine learning models.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically analyzes the expressibility-trainability relationship in hybrid quantum neural networks (HQNNs) and finds that the assumed trade-off between these properties in pure PQCs is weak and regime-dependent, while hybrid architectures further disrupt and can eliminate this relationship. The authors propose a multi-objective neural architecture search (NAS) framework to jointly optimize expressibility, trainability, and task performance across the classical-quantum design space, showing that hybridization fundamentally reshapes the optimization landscape.
AI.motivation: The commonly assumed trade-off between expressibility and trainability (where highly expressive PQCs suffer more from barren plateaus) has been well-studied in pure quantum circuits, but its validity in hybrid quantum neural networks (where PQCs are embedded within classical networks) remains unclear. The authors aim to systematically investigate this relationship in HQNNs under various training configurations.
AI.method: The authors systematically analyze PQCs across varying circuit depths, qubit counts, and entanglement topologies under three training configurations: (1) pure PQCs, (2) quantum-only training in a hybrid setting, and (3) full end-to-end training of hybrid models. They also propose a multi-objective neural architecture search (NAS) framework that jointly optimizes expressibility, trainability, and task performance over a combined classical-quantum design space.
AI.result: Pure PQCs exhibit only a weak and regime-dependent expressibility-trainability trade-off. Hybrid architectures increasingly disrupt and can eliminate this trade-off under full hybrid training, indicating that classical components reshape the optimization landscape and decouple trainability from PQC expressibility. The NAS framework reveals different Pareto-optimal solutions depending on the training configuration and trainability definitions used.
AI.conclusion: Hybridization is not just an implementation detail but a defining factor in quantum machine learning model performance. The classical components in HQNNs fundamentally alter the optimization landscape, breaking the assumed coupling between expressibility and trainability.

title: Q-RAIL: A Reliability-Aware Framework for Quantum Federated Learning on Heterogeneous Noisy Hardware
summary: Quantum federated learning (QFL) on NISQ hardware is highly sensitive to backend heterogeneity: some clients contribute informative updates, while others contribute noise-dominated drift that uniform averaging cannot distinguish. We propose Q-RAIL (Quantum Reliability-Aware Federated Inference and Learning), a circuit- and calibration-aware aggregation method for hardware-heterogeneous QFL. Q-RAIL computes a client-specific effective noise budget from backend calibration metadata together with transpiled circuit statistics. This budget is converted into stabilized aggregation weights using temperature scaling, uniform mixing, and a minimum-weight floor. Q-RAIL was evaluated across multiple experimental settings, including an ablation study, and benchmarked against state-of-the-art methods on three datasets: MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and OrganAMNIST. On the primary MNIST benchmark under strong hardware skew, Q-RAIL improves final test accuracy from FedAvg's 0.777 to 0.877, a +10.0-point gain corresponding to about 44.8% relative error reduction, while also exceeding the strongest wpQFL baseline (0.833). At the same time, test loss drops from 0.722 to 0.585, and test AUC rises from 0.920 to 0.973. Under non-IID MNIST, Q-RAIL reaches 0.813 vs 0.722 for FedAvg. It also outperforms FedAvg in 12/12 ansatz/CX-fold stress configurations and remains stronger at 4, 10, and 15 qubit setups. Overall, the results support calibration-driven, circuit-aware aggregation as a practical path toward robust QFL on heterogeneous quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: Q-RAIL is a calibration- and circuit-aware aggregation method for quantum federated learning on heterogeneous NISQ hardware. It computes client-specific effective noise budgets from backend calibration metadata and transpiled circuit statistics, converting them into stabilized aggregation weights. On MNIST under hardware skew, Q-RAIL improves test accuracy from FedAvg's 0.777 to 0.877 (44.8% relative error reduction), surpassing wpQFL (0.833), and shows consistent gains across datasets, non-IID settings, and varied qubit configurations.
AI.motivation: Quantum federated learning on NISQ hardware suffers from backend heterogeneity, where some clients provide informative updates while others contribute noise-dominated drift. Standard uniform averaging (e.g., FedAvg) cannot distinguish between these, motivating a need for reliability-aware, circuit- and calibration-driven aggregation.
AI.method: Q-RAIL computes a client-specific effective noise budget using backend calibration metadata and transpiled circuit statistics. These budgets are converted into stabilized aggregation weights via temperature scaling, uniform mixing, and a minimum-weight floor, enabling noise-aware differentiation among clients.
AI.result: On MNIST under strong hardware skew: accuracy 0.877 (FedAvg: 0.777, wpQFL: 0.833); loss 0.585 (FedAvg: 0.722); AUC 0.973 (FedAvg: 0.920). Under non-IID MNIST: 0.813 vs 0.722. Outperforms FedAvg in 12/12 ansatz/CX-fold stress configurations and remains stronger at 4, 10, and 15 qubit setups.
AI.conclusion: Calibration-driven, circuit-aware aggregation provides a practical path toward robust QFL on heterogeneous quantum hardware, effectively mitigating the impact of noise-dominated client updates.

title: Boundary $0/π$ logical subspace and bulk dynamical probes in flux-controlled anomalous Floquet quantum walks
summary: We formulate a one-dimensional flux-controlled anomalous Floquet quantum walk and show that it admits a direct microscopic realization in a driven bipartite lattice. The walk consists of a coin-dependent drift step and a momentum-dependent coin mixing step, so the same evolution operator governs quasienergy bands, boundary modes, and bulk dynamics in real space. Because the walk is chiral, the quasienergy gaps at $0$ and $π/T$ carry independent topological information, which organizes trivial, $0$-only, $π$-only, and coexistence sectors in the $(M,φ)$ plane. In the coexistence sector, a $0$ mode and a $π$ mode reside on the same edge and span a natural boundary logical subspace. One Floquet period acts there as a relative phase operation and produces a clear $2T$ response in local boundary observables. In the bulk, the same anomalous Floquet structure is probed dynamically in two complementary ways. Frame-resolved mean chiral displacements approach the two winding numbers in the clean pre-reflection window of the symmetric time frames, while selected benchmark cuts at a representative $0$ gap closing and a representative $π$ gap closing exhibit distinct local stroboscopic responses, with the $π$ gap benchmark showing a much stronger odd-even alternation. The boundary logical subspace and the bulk dynamical probes are therefore organized within one flux-controlled anomalous Floquet quantum walk, suggesting a symmetry-protected route to quantum-walk information primitives in driven microstructured lattices.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates a one-dimensional flux-controlled anomalous Floquet quantum walk in a driven bipartite lattice, demonstrating that its chiral symmetry organizes topological phases (trivial, 0-only, π-only, and coexistence sectors) in the (M,φ) plane. In the coexistence sector, 0 and π edge modes on the same edge form a logical subspace, with Floquet periods acting as relative phase operations and producing a 2T response. Bulk dynamical probes (frame-resolved mean chiral displacements and stroboscopic responses) reveal the two winding numbers, linking boundary logical subspaces with bulk topological probes.
AI.motivation: To realize a microscopically driven bipartite lattice implementation of an anomalous Floquet quantum walk with flux control, where independent topological information at 0 and π/T gaps can organize distinct topological sectors and support a boundary logical subspace for quantum information primitives.
AI.method: The method involves formulating a one-dimensional flux-controlled anomalous Floquet quantum walk with coin-dependent drift and momentum-dependent coin mixing, realized in a driven bipartite lattice. The chiral symmetry enables independent topological characterization at 0 and π gaps. Bulk dynamics are probed via frame-resolved mean chiral displacements in symmetric time frames and via local stroboscopic measurements at selected gap-closing benchmarks.
AI.result: The (M,φ) phase diagram organizes into trivial, 0-only, π-only, and coexistence sectors. In the coexistence sector, 0 and π modes coexist on the same edge, forming a logical subspace with a 2T response. Frame-resolved mean chiral displacements extract two winding numbers in the clean pre-reflection window. The π-gap benchmark exhibits a significantly stronger odd-even alternation in stroboscopic response compared to the 0-gap benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The boundary logical subspace and bulk dynamical probes are unified within a single flux-controlled anomalous Floquet quantum walk, suggesting a symmetry-protected route to quantum-walk-based information primitives in driven microstructured lattices.

title: Sideband fingerprints of antibunched light in cascaded quantum wave mixing
summary: Quantum wave mixing on a single superconducting qubit produces a hierarchy of coherent side peaks associated with elastic multiphoton scattering pathways. In a cascaded source--probe geometry these pathways become sensitive to the photon statistics of the radiation emitted by the source qubit. We develop an analytical theory of this effect starting from the cascaded master equation in the weak-driving regime. In the coherent-filtering limit $γ_{\rm s}\ggγ_{\rm pr}$, the standard coherent--coherent wave-mixing hierarchy is recovered. In the opposite limit $γ_{\rm pr}\ggγ_{\rm s}$, side peaks associated with multiphoton absorption from the antibunched source field are parametrically suppressed. Numerical solutions confirm the analytical scaling laws. The resulting sideband hierarchy provides a frequency-domain fingerprint of antibunched itinerant microwave light.

AI.tldr: Quantum wave mixing on a single superconducting qubit produces coherent side peaks sensitive to source photon statistics; in the weak-driving regime, an analytical theory from the cascaded master equation reveals that multiphoton absorption side peaks are suppressed when probe decay dominates source decay, providing a frequency-domain fingerprint of antibunched microwave light.
AI.motivation: To understand how the photon statistics of a source qubit affect the coherent wave-mixing side peak hierarchy in a cascaded source-probe geometry, and to develop an analytical theory for this effect.
AI.method: Analytical theory derived from the cascaded master equation in the weak-driving regime, with numerical solutions for validation. Two limits are analyzed: coherent-filtering (γ_s ≫ γ_pr) and antibunched-source (γ_pr ≫ γ_s).
AI.result: In the coherent-filtering limit, the standard coherent-coherent wave-mixing hierarchy is recovered. In the opposite limit where probe decay dominates, multiphoton absorption side peaks from the antibunched source are parametrically suppressed. Numerical solutions confirm the analytical scaling laws.
AI.conclusion: The sideband hierarchy serves as a frequency-domain fingerprint of antibunched itinerant microwave light, enabling characterization of photon statistics through spectral measurements.

title: Utility-scale quantum experiments using dynamic circuits to address collective dissipation in interacting qubits
summary: Open quantum systems are central to quantum optics, condensed matter, and chemistry, yet their simulation remains challenging for both classical and near-term quantum hardware. In this work we implement and execute utility-scale quantum circuits that accurately reproduce the dissipative dynamics of interacting qubits. We consider a one-dimensional chain of many qubits weakly coupled to a common Markovian bath. The Markovian time evolution of the system is implemented through Trotterized evolution with the introduction of ancilla-assisted dissipative channels, including single-qubit and two-qubit dissipators to capture collective decay. Mid-circuit measurements, conditional gates, and hardware-aware transpilation significantly reduce circuit depth. We further implement a biased Clifford data regression (biased CDR), an error mitigation strategy that outperforms the uniform Cliffordization baseline and a variety of zero-noise extrapolation protocols. We execute large-scale quantum experiments of the dynamics of chains comprising up to 86 emitters on the IBM System Two \texttt{ibm\_basquecountry}. In order to do so, we use 129 total qubits (including ancillas), with the largest circuits contain about 8000 two-qubit gates. To validate these experiments we develop a classical Monte Carlo-Time-Evolving Block-Decimation (MC-TEBD) tensor-network method that incorporates reset operations through stochastic pure-state trajectories, obtaining very good agreement. The approach presented here opens a practical route for utility-scale quantum simulation of dissipative dynamics, enabled by dynamic circuits, targeted error mitigation, and tensor-network validation, and enables to tackle complex dynamics of systems such as quantum emitters in dissipative optical cavities.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates utility-scale quantum simulation of open quantum systems (dissipative dynamics) on IBM quantum hardware using 129 qubits, dynamic circuits, ancilla-assisted dissipation, and biased CDR error mitigation, validated by classical MC-TEBD tensor-network simulations.
AI.motivation: Simulating open quantum systems (interacting qubits coupled to a Markovian bath) is classically challenging and remains difficult for near-term quantum hardware. The authors aim to demonstrate practical utility-scale quantum simulation of dissipative dynamics on current quantum processors.
AI.method: The authors implement Trotterized evolution with ancilla-assisted dissipative channels (single- and two-qubit dissipators) to model collective decay. Mid-circuit measurements, conditional gates, and hardware-aware transpilation reduce circuit depth. Biased Clifford data regression (biased CDR) is used for error mitigation. Validation uses a classical MC-TEBD tensor-network method with stochastic pure-state trajectories incorporating reset operations.
AI.result: Experiments simulate chains of up to 86 emitters on IBM System Two (ibm_basquecountry), using 129 total qubits. Largest circuits contain ~8000 two-qubit gates. Biased CDR outperforms uniform Cliffordization and zero-noise extrapolation. Good agreement is found with classical MC-TEBD simulations.
AI.conclusion: The work opens a practical route for utility-scale quantum simulation of dissipative dynamics, enabled by dynamic circuits, targeted error mitigation, and tensor-network validation, applicable to complex systems like quantum emitters in dissipative optical cavities.

title: A Variational Dissipative Framework for Quantum Algorithms
summary: Dissipation engineering has attracted growing interest as an approach to controlling open quantum systems through engineered system-environment interactions. Standard variational quantum circuits are usually built from unitary operations and therefore explore only a restricted family of states. To go beyond this limitation, we introduce a variational dissipative framework in which ancilla-assisted engineered dissipation is incorporated into parameterized quantum algorithms. In this framework, system-only variational layers are combined with trainable dissipative modules, so that the circuit can prepare a broader class of mixed states through ancilla-assisted nonunitary transformations. Within this framework, the same ancilla-assisted dissipative block is used in two representative settings with different objectives. For ground-state search, it is integrated into a dissipative variational quantum eigensolver to improve the convergence toward low-energy states. For state recovery, it is trained as a recovery channel to suppress preparation noise and enhance fidelity with the target state. In both cases, the block is realized through parameterized system-ancilla couplings followed by ancilla reset and trace-out. Our results show that engineered dissipation can be incorporated into variational quantum circuits as a reusable trainable primitive rather than treated only as a source of noise. In this sense, the proposed framework identifies ancilla-assisted dissipative channels as a concrete variational resource that can support both optimization and recovery tasks within a unified design.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a variational dissipative framework that incorporates ancilla-assisted engineered dissipation into parameterized quantum circuits, enabling the preparation of a broader class of mixed states. This unified design uses the same dissipative block for both ground-state search (via a dissipative variational quantum eigensolver) and state recovery (as a trainable recovery channel), demonstrating that engineered dissipation can serve as a reusable variational resource rather than merely a source of noise.
AI.motivation: Standard variational quantum circuits rely solely on unitary operations, limiting the family of states they can explore. The authors aim to overcome this restriction by incorporating engineered dissipation to access a broader class of mixed states.
AI.method: The framework combines system-only variational layers with trainable dissipative modules realized through parameterized system-ancilla couplings, followed by ancilla reset and trace-out operations. The same ancilla-assisted dissipative block is applied in two settings: (1) a dissipative variational quantum eigensolver for ground-state search, and (2) a trainable recovery channel for state recovery from preparation noise.
AI.result: Engineered dissipation improves convergence toward low-energy states in ground-state search and enhances fidelity with target states in state recovery tasks. The dissipative block functions as a reusable trainable primitive within variational quantum algorithms.
AI.conclusion: Ancilla-assisted dissipative channels serve as a concrete variational resource that can support both optimization and recovery tasks within a unified design, shifting the perspective on dissipation from a source of noise to a useful engineering tool.

title: Steady-state phases in long-range measurement-only quantum circuits
summary: Measurements can drive quantum many-body systems into nontrivial steady states and induce interesting dynamical phase transitions, rendering measurement-only quantum circuits a useful platform for exploring quantum many-body phases beyond those of equilibrium Hamiltonian systems. Here we study a class of long-range measurement-only quantum circuits with competing two-qubit and three-qubit measurements. We demonstrate that these circuits exhibit rich steady-state structure and uncover a strong influence of the measurement range on the resulting phases. In particular, states with symmetry-protected topological (SPT) order can emerge with sufficiently short-range measurements beyond the nearest-neighbor limit. These states feature robust topological edge modes, which can also be detected from circuit dynamics. With longer-range measurements, an extended parameter regime emerges in which conventional order parameters are suppressed while spatial correlations remain nontrivial. Moreover, we show that in this circuit model sufficiently long-range measurements can produce significant entanglement with scaling beyond an area law despite the absence of any unitary evolution.

AI.tldr: Long-range measurement-only quantum circuits with competing two- and three-qubit measurements exhibit rich steady-state phases, including symmetry-protected topological order with short-range measurements, a regime with suppressed order but nontrivial correlations at intermediate range, and entanglement beyond area law at long range—all without unitary evolution.
AI.motivation: To explore quantum many-body phases beyond equilibrium Hamiltonian systems by studying measurement-only quantum circuits and to understand how measurement range influences steady-state structure and phase transitions.
AI.method: Class of long-range measurement-only quantum circuits with competing two-qubit and three-qubit measurements, analyzed as a function of measurement range.
AI.result: Short-range measurements yield symmetry-protected topological (SPT) order with robust edge modes; intermediate-range measurements suppress conventional order while preserving nontrivial spatial correlations; sufficiently long-range measurements produce entanglement scaling beyond area law without unitary evolution.
AI.conclusion: Measurement range is a key control parameter that enables nontrivial steady-state phases—including SPT order and volume-law-like entanglement—solely via measurements, expanding the landscape of measurement-induced phases.

title: Photon position eigenstates in configuration space
summary: The expressions of the eigenfunctions of the Hawton photon position operator in the configuration space are derived for several classes of wave function, including the Riemann-Silberstein and Landau-Peierls cases. Although these eigenfunctions have a simple form in momentum space, the explicit characterization of their representations in the configuration space is rather more involved. We provide closed expressions of these eigenfunctions in terms of linear combinations of the complete elliptic integrals $K(κ)$ and $E(κ)$ with modulus $κ$ depending on trigonometric functions of the polar angle. We show that they diverge not only at the value $\mathbf q$ of the position eigenvalue, but also on a plane containing $\mathbf q$ and that they decay as inverse powers of the distance from $\mathbf q$.

AI.tldr: This paper derives closed-form expressions for Hawton photon position operator eigenfunctions in configuration space, showing they diverge at the eigenvalue and on a plane containing it, while decaying as inverse powers of distance.
AI.motivation: To explicitly characterize the configuration space representations of eigenfunctions of the Hawton photon position operator, which have simple momentum-space forms but complex spatial representations.
AI.method: Closed expressions derived using linear combinations of complete elliptic integrals K(κ) and E(κ) with moduli depending on trigonometric functions of the polar angle.
AI.result: Eigenfunctions diverge at the position eigenvalue q and on a plane containing q, and decay as inverse powers of distance from q.
AI.conclusion: The eigenfunctions of the Hawton photon position operator are expressed analytically for Riemann-Silberstein and Landau-Peierls wave function classes, revealing singular behavior on a plane and algebraic decay.

title: Geometric Quantization on Orbifolds
summary: This text introduces geometric quantization on orbifolds. After reviewing the necessary background, it develops new treatments of prequantization, polarizations, and metaplectic correction for symplectic orbifolds.

AI.tldr: This paper develops geometric quantization theory for symplectic orbifolds, covering prequantization, polarizations, and metaplectic correction.
AI.motivation: To extend geometric quantization, originally formulated for smooth symplectic manifolds, to the setting of symplectic orbifolds, which have mild singularities.
AI.method: Reviews background on orbifolds and symplectic geometry, then develops new treatments of prequantization (line bundles with connection), polarizations (choice of Lagrangian foliation), and metaplectic correction (half-form bundles) adapted to the orbifold context.
AI.result: Provides a systematic framework for geometric quantization on symplectic orbifolds.
AI.conclusion: Geometric quantization can be extended to orbifolds, potentially enabling quantum theories on spaces with quotient singularities.

title: Bargmann Zeros as a Diagnostic of the Tunneling Transition in Double-Well Quantum Systems
summary: Complex zeros of wavefunctions represented as entire functions in Bargmann--Fock space encode structural information about the underlying quantum state. Prior work employed zero galleries of randomly generated polynomial superpositions of Fock states as visual fingerprints suitable for classification. Here we examine whether Bargmann zeros of physically realized eigenstates of one-dimensional anharmonic and double-well Hamiltonians carry a recognizable signature of the tunneling transition in the symmetric double well. Ground and first-excited eigenstates are obtained from a variational ansatz consisting of a physically motivated symbolic envelope multiplied by a small flexible correction network, trained by Rayleigh--Ritz minimization of the finite-difference Hamiltonian expectation value and validated to reproduce energies to within $\sim 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{Ha}$. The resulting wavefunctions are projected onto the harmonic-oscillator basis and the complex zeros of the truncated Bargmann polynomial are located by numerical root-finding. For harmonic and quartic-anharmonic potentials the zeros show no preferred orientation. For double-well eigenstates, by contrast, the zeros condense onto the imaginary axis. A sweep of the barrier parameter $a$ from $0.5$ to $2.3$ reveals a continuous migration of zeros toward the imaginary axis, concurrent with the exponential collapse of the tunneling splitting $Δ(a) = E_1 - E_0$ over $3.5$ decades. This condensation is traced to a sign-alternation pattern in the Fock-coefficient spectrum that is characteristic of bimodally localized wavefunctions. The complex zero set of the Bargmann-represented wavefunction thereby provides a compact, purely analytic diagnostic for the tunneling regime of one-dimensional double-well Hamiltonians, extending the random-polynomial zero-image framework to physical eigenstates.

AI.tldr: Complex zeros of Bargmann-represented wavefunctions for symmetric double-well eigenstates condense onto the imaginary axis as the barrier parameter increases, correlating with the exponential collapse of tunneling splitting. This zero-axis condensation, traced to sign-alternation in Fock coefficients, provides an analytic diagnostic for tunneling regimes.
AI.motivation: To determine whether Bargmann zeros of physically realized eigenstates carry a recognizable signature of the tunneling transition in symmetric double-well potentials, extending prior work on random polynomial zero galleries to physical quantum states.
AI.method: Variational ansatz (symbolic envelope + flexible correction network) trained by Rayleigh-Ritz minimization of finite-difference Hamiltonian expectation value; projection onto harmonic-oscillator basis; numerical root-finding of truncated Bargmann polynomial zeros; sweep of double-well barrier parameter a from 0.5 to 2.3.
AI.result: Harmonic and quartic-anharmonic zeros show no preferred orientation. Double-well eigenstate zeros condense onto the imaginary axis as barrier parameter increases, concurrent with tunneling splitting Δ(a) collapsing over 3.5 decades. Condensation originates from sign-alternation in Fock coefficients characteristic of bimodally localized wavefunctions.
AI.conclusion: Complex zero sets of Bargmann-represented wavefunctions serve as a compact, purely analytic diagnostic for the tunneling regime in 1D double-well Hamiltonians, extending random-polynomial zero-image frameworks to physically realized eigenstates.

title: Implementation of distillation protocols using a recirculating bricks mesh network
summary: General-purpose programmable photonic processors provide a flexible foundation for integrating various functionalities within a single chip. A two-dimensional bricks waveguide mesh of Mach Zehnder interferometers has been demonstrated to possess considerable potential in the domain of photonic neural networks and quantum signal processing. In this article, we propose an expansion of the available applications of recirculating bricks mesh architecture to distillation protocols necessary for quantum signal processing. These protocols are essential for the heralding of the output of single photons, which is characterized by a reduced distinguishability error rate. The demonstration will be made of a single programmable optical system's ability to realize various distillation protocols with reduced computational resource costs. The present study will concentrate on cascaded quantum interferometers and Fourier transform-based schemes. It will demonstrate that the bricks mesh can implement such schemes, which are unattainable using feed-forward networks, without the need for complex out-of-plane integration. The propagation of the signal in any direction, along with the utilization of all ports as both input and output, facilitates the execution of such transformations with minimal optical depth of the circuit and in time scales shorter than the decoherence time.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using a two-dimensional bricks waveguide mesh of Mach-Zehnder interferometers—a programmable photonic processor—to implement distillation protocols for quantum signal processing, specifically for heralding single photons with reduced distinguishability error, achieving capabilities unattainable with feed-forward networks while maintaining low optical depth and operation within decoherence time.
AI.motivation: To expand the applications of the recirculating bricks mesh architecture to distillation protocols needed for quantum signal processing, particularly for heralding single-photon outputs with reduced error rates, and to demonstrate that a single programmable photonic system can realize various distillation protocols with lower computational resource costs.
AI.method: The study focuses on cascaded quantum interferometers and Fourier transform-based schemes implemented on a 2D bricks waveguide mesh of Mach-Zehnder interferometers, where the mesh's bidirectional signal propagation and flexible port usage enable complex transformations without out-of-plane integration or feed-forward network limitations.
AI.result: The bricks mesh architecture can implement distillation protocols (cascaded quantum interferometers and Fourier-based schemes) that are impossible with feed-forward networks, without requiring complex out-of-plane integration, while achieving minimal optical depth and operation times shorter than decoherence time.
AI.conclusion: The recirculating bricks mesh is a versatile platform capable of executing quantum distillation protocols efficiently, with reduced computational cost and hardware complexity, making it suitable for quantum signal processing applications.

title: Native topological readout on qubit hardware: a Fibonacci-chain benchmark of measurement-compilation trade-offs
summary: Recent demonstrations of non-Abelian braiding of graph vertices on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) superconducting processor, and the experimental realization of topological order in general on various quantum hardware platforms necessitate an important question: when does a native (topological) fusion readout genuinely help for topological anyonic Hamiltonians implemented on NISQ hardware? We use the Fibonacci anyons chain as a concrete model for understanding the trade-off between measurement cost and compilation cost in that setting. The comparison is made against a simple grouped-Pauli baseline, and is scored by a covariance-aware mean-squared-error (MSE) of the full energy estimator. We based our benchmark on two different important classes of quantum circuits, namely Floquet time-evolved and variational quantum eigensolver quantum circuits, with the underlying Hamiltonian consisting of both braiding and fusion interaction. Our analysis found that there is not a uniform best method across both problems: the fusion readout method performed better on Floquet-type circuits on both the MSE and covariance-aware sampling variance, while the grouped Pauli method performed better on VQE on the MSE but worse on sampling variance. We derive scaling laws, and compute shot-budget crossover points, where one method is operationally favored above the other. The relevance of this work extends beyond Fibonacci chains to two-dimensional topological models compiled on superconducting and other qubit-native platforms, and can be used as a guide in answering the question of when one should measure in the native operator basis of the target physics, or when it is better to fall back on Pauli-basis reconstruction.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes when fusion readout (native topological measurement) vs. grouped-Pauli readout is more efficient for simulating topological anyonic Hamiltonians on NISQ hardware, using Fibonacci anyon chains as a testbed. The comparison considers Floquet and VQE circuits, finding that fusion readout performs better on Floquet circuits, while grouped-Pauli performs better on VQE circuits in terms of MSE, with crossover points analyzed.
AI.motivation: Given recent demonstrations of non-Abelian braiding and topological order on NISQ processors, there is a practical need to understand when native topological fusion readout genuinely outperforms simpler Pauli-basis reconstruction for measuring anyonic Hamiltonians implemented on quantum hardware.
AI.method: Using the Fibonacci anyon chain as a concrete model, the authors compare fusion readout against a grouped-Pauli baseline, evaluated via covariance-aware MSE of the full energy estimator. Benchmarks are performed on two circuit classes: Floquet time-evolved circuits and variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) circuits, with Hamiltonians containing both braiding and fusion interactions.
AI.result: No single method is universally better: fusion readout outperforms grouped-Pauli on Floquet circuits in both MSE and covariance-aware sampling variance; grouped-Pauli performs better on VQE in MSE but worse in sampling variance. Scaling laws and shot-budget crossover points are derived to determine operational preference.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a practical guide for deciding when to use native operator basis (fusion) measurement vs. Pauli-basis reconstruction on NISQ hardware, extending beyond Fibonacci chains to 2D topological models on superconducting and other qubit platforms.

title: Unified Flux Control Architecture for Fluxonium Qubits
summary: Control architectures that reduce hardware overhead while maintaining high-fidelity operations are essential for the continued scaling of superconducting quantum processors. Here we experimentally realize a unified control architecture for fluxonium qubits, in which both transverse ($XY$) and longitudinal ($Z$) operations are implemented through a single flux-control channel driven by a single arbitrary waveform generator channel. This architecture imposes competing requirements on the shared control channel, which must simultaneously support low-frequency flux transmission for reset operations while strongly attenuating broadband noise near the qubit transition frequency. We address this challenge through frequency-selective cryogenic filtering together with compensated waveform synthesis that corrects the pulse distortion introduced by the filtered control line. Experimentally, this approach preserves coherence times above 100 $μ$s while enabling active reset with approximately 98% fidelity and 20-ns single-qubit gates with fidelities exceeding 99.99%. We further demonstrate FPGA-native instruction-level waveform synthesis based on reusable pulse primitives for unified flux control. These results establish unified flux control as a scalable architecture for fluxonium qubits that reduces control hardware overhead while preserving high-fidelity operation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a unified flux-control architecture for fluxonium qubits that uses a single flux-control channel for both XY and Z operations, achieving high-fidelity gates and reset through cryogenic filtering and compensated waveform synthesis, demonstrating a scalable approach to reduce control hardware overhead.
AI.motivation: Control architectures that reduce hardware overhead while maintaining high-fidelity operations are essential for scaling superconducting quantum processors.
AI.method: The authors implement a unified control architecture using a single flux-control channel driven by one arbitrary waveform generator channel for both transverse (XY) and longitudinal (Z) operations. They employ frequency-selective cryogenic filtering and compensated waveform synthesis to correct pulse distortion, along with FPGA-native instruction-level waveform synthesis using reusable pulse primitives.
AI.result: Coherence times above 100 μs, active reset with approximately 98% fidelity, 20-ns single-qubit gates with fidelities exceeding 99.99%.
AI.conclusion: Unified flux control is established as a scalable architecture for fluxonium qubits that reduces control hardware overhead while preserving high-fidelity operation.

title: PauLIB: A High-Performance Library for Processing Pauli Strings
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE QCE
summary: Processing large Pauli sums is a significant bottleneck in quantum chemistry, Pauli propagation, and Pauli-based compilation. Existing frameworks often suffer from Python interpreter overhead or utilize hash-map data structures that hinder SIMD vectorization and complicate multi-threaded merging. We present PauLIB, a header-only C++20 library designed to eliminate these bottlenecks through three key architectural choices. A bit-packed binary symplectic representation that encodes each qubit in two bits, reducing Pauli multiplication to a bitwise XOR and a population count; a sorted array layout that replaces hash maps to enable branch-predictable SIMD bulk operations; and a struct-of-arrays (SoA) memory layout that exposes contiguous word arrays for explicit SIMD vectorization. Benchmarks at 500 qubits show that single Pauli string multiplication runs at 25ns per operation-14 times faster than PauliEngine and 660 times faster than Qiskit-flat across all pair counts tested. Hamiltonian outer-product multiplication is approximately 10 times faster than PauliEngine and 45 times faster than Qiskit at all tested sizes. Greedy commutation grouping, the dominant preprocessing cost in variational algorithms, achieves up to 21,000 times speedup over PennyLane, driven by the compact bit-packed representation. The compact layout reduces the memory footprint of a one-million-term Hamiltonian at 500 qubits from 1,036MB (Qiskit) to 142MB, a 7.3 times reduction that directly enables larger problem sizes within a fixed memory budget. PauLIB is open source and provides C++ and Python interfaces.

AI.tldr: PauLIB is a header-only C++20 library that uses a bit-packed binary symplectic representation, sorted array layout, and struct-of-arrays memory layout to achieve dramatic speedups (up to 21,000x) and memory reductions (7.3x) for Pauli sum processing in quantum computing workloads.
AI.motivation: Processing large Pauli sums is a significant bottleneck in quantum chemistry, Pauli propagation, and Pauli-based compilation. Existing frameworks suffer from Python interpreter overhead or use hash-map data structures that hinder SIMD vectorization and complicate multi-threaded merging.
AI.method: PauLIB employs three key architectural choices: (1) a bit-packed binary symplectic representation encoding each qubit in two bits, reducing Pauli multiplication to bitwise XOR and population count; (2) a sorted array layout replacing hash maps for branch-predictable SIMD bulk operations; and (3) a struct-of-arrays (SoA) memory layout exposing contiguous word arrays for explicit SIMD vectorization.
AI.result: Single Pauli string multiplication runs at 25ns per operation (14x faster than PauliEngine, 660x faster than Qiskit-flat); Hamiltonian outer-product multiplication is ~10x faster than PauliEngine and 45x faster than Qiskit; greedy commutation grouping achieves up to 21,000x speedup over PennyLane; memory footprint of a one-million-term Hamiltonian at 500 qubits reduced from 1,036MB (Qiskit) to 142MB (7.3x reduction).
AI.conclusion: PauLIB eliminates Pauli sum processing bottlenecks through compact representation and SIMD-friendly data layouts, enabling larger problem sizes within fixed memory budgets. The library is open source with both C++ and Python interfaces.

title: Evaluating System-Level Fidelity with Peaked Random Circuits
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Quantum computing is transitioning from experimental prototypes to commercially available turnkey systems, making architecture-agnostic performance metrics essential for cross-platform comparison. Peaked Random Circuits (PRCs) have recently been proposed as a viable path to demonstrate quantum advantage on NISQ devices: a quantum processor can reliably detect a single, peaked output state amid background noise, yet the circuits' characteristics render classical simulation infeasible. In this paper, we repurpose PRCs as a system-level fidelity benchmark. By successively running a matrix of PRCs with varying qubit counts and circuit depths, we quantify a system's ability to identify the deterministic peak despite cumulative noise, gate errors, and connectivity constraints. We apply the benchmark on IQM's superconducting and AQT's trapped-ion architectures. Our results show that PRCs provide a high-precision metric comparable to Quantum Volume while exhibiting greater sensitivity to interference effects. Consequently, PRCs enable a robust framework for assessing the computational reliability of NISQ hardware across platforms.

AI.tldr: Peaked Random Circuits (PRCs) are repurposed as a system-level fidelity benchmark for NISQ devices, providing a high-precision, architecture-agnostic metric that is more sensitive to interference effects than Quantum Volume, demonstrated on superconducting and trapped-ion architectures.
AI.motivation: Quantum computing is moving from experimental to commercial systems, requiring architecture-agnostic performance metrics for cross-platform comparison. Existing benchmarks like Quantum Volume may lack sensitivity to certain noise characteristics.
AI.method: PRCs are repurposed as a system-level fidelity benchmark by running a matrix of circuits with varying qubit counts and depths. The benchmark quantifies a system's ability to identify the deterministic peak output amid noise, gate errors, and connectivity constraints. Applied to IQM's superconducting and AQT's trapped-ion architectures.
AI.result: PRCs provide a high-precision metric comparable to Quantum Volume while exhibiting greater sensitivity to interference effects. Demonstrated on two different quantum hardware architectures (superconducting and trapped-ion).
AI.conclusion: PRCs enable a robust framework for assessing computational reliability of NISQ hardware across different platforms, offering improved sensitivity to interference compared to existing benchmarks.

title: Training-Free Quantum Generative Paradigm via Local Parent Hamiltonians
summary: We propose a training-free quantum generative paradigm, which is fundamentally different from current generative models, which demand substantial computational power, face practical scalability limits, and often function as opaque black boxes, despite their remarkable success. We enable image and text generation without parameter training, by constructing a local parent Hamiltonian whose ground state encodes the target distribution and then solving the global Hamiltonian. Rooted directly in quantum mechanical principles, this approach establishes a new pathway for generative modeling that leverages superposition and entanglement to maintain global consistency.

AI.tldr: A training-free quantum generative paradigm that constructs local parent Hamiltonians to encode target distributions and generates images/text by solving global Hamiltonians, leveraging quantum superposition and entanglement for global consistency without parameter training.
AI.motivation: Current generative models require substantial computational power, face scalability limits, and operate as opaque black boxes. This work aims to establish a fundamentally new pathway that circumvents these limitations by grounding generative modeling directly in quantum mechanical principles.
AI.method: Constructs a local parent Hamiltonian whose ground state encodes the target distribution, then solves the global Hamiltonian to generate samples. No parameter training is involved; generation is achieved through quantum mechanical solving of the Hamiltonian system.
AI.result: Enables image and text generation without parameter training by leveraging quantum superposition and entanglement to maintain global consistency across generated outputs.
AI.conclusion: This training-free quantum generative paradigm offers a fundamentally different approach to generative modeling, rooted directly in quantum mechanics, potentially addressing key limitations of current models including computational demands, scalability, and opacity.

title: Toward General Quantum Control with Physics-Informed Large Language Models
summary: Quantum control is essential for quantum information science and technology, yet designing high-fidelity control protocols remains challenging due to complex optimization landscapes, hardware noise, and long pulse sequences. Existing numerical solvers often require problem-specific engineering and produce opaque control amplitudes, while naive large language models (LLMs) lack the physical consistency and long-horizon precision for reliable quantum control synthesis. Here we introduce VF-QCTRL, a physics-informed large language model framework for general quantum control that combines symbolic reasoning with optimization to propose analytic control ansätze and coherently refine their parameters through feedback. To systematically evaluate LLM-driven quantum control, we develop QCTRL-BENCH, a benchmark spanning sixteen tasks across single- and multi-qubit systems, closed and open quantum dynamics, noiseless and noisy settings, and both analytic and numerical protocols. Across the benchmark, VF-QCTRL demonstrates strong universality, accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability: it applies to generic quantum control systems without task-specific training, achieves performance competitive with or exceeding state-of-the-art conventional solvers in both noiseless and noisy regimes with query efficiency, exhibits favorable inference-time scaling and pulse resolution scaling, and derives physically interpretable analytical protocols directly from prompts. Our results establish physics-informed LLM-based quantum control as a promising paradigm for accurate, efficient, interpretable, and training-free quantum control protocol design across a broad range of quantum systems.

AI.tldr: VF-QCTRL is a physics-informed LLM framework for quantum control that combines symbolic reasoning with optimization to design and refine control protocols, achieving competitive or superior performance across a comprehensive benchmark (QCTRL-BENCH) spanning 16 tasks, demonstrating universality, accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability without task-specific training.
AI.motivation: Designing high-fidelity quantum control protocols is challenging due to complex optimization landscapes, hardware noise, and long pulse sequences; existing numerical solvers are problem-specific and produce opaque solutions, while naive LLMs lack physical consistency and precision for reliable quantum control synthesis.
AI.method: VF-QCTRL combines symbolic reasoning with optimization to propose analytic control ansätze and coherently refine parameters through feedback, using a physics-informed LLM framework. The authors also introduce QCTRL-BENCH, a benchmark covering single-/multi-qubit systems, closed/open dynamics, noiseless/noisy settings, and analytic/numerical protocols across 16 tasks.
AI.result: VF-QCTRL achieves strong universality (applies generically without task-specific training), accuracy (competitive with or exceeding state-of-the-art solvers), efficiency (query efficiency, favorable inference-time scaling, and pulse resolution scaling), and interpretability (deriving physically interpretable analytical protocols directly from prompts) across the benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Physics-informed LLM-based quantum control represents a promising paradigm for accurate, efficient, interpretable, and training-free quantum control protocol design across a broad range of quantum systems.

title: Asymptotically Optimal Depth Fermionic Permutation on 2D Grid Quantum Architecture without Ancillas
summary: Simulating fermionic systems on qubit hardware involves many nonlocal interactions, and efficient routing of these interactions is critical to the overall cost of fermionic simulation algorithms. Recent works reduce this Jordan-Wigner routing overhead to polylogarithmic depth under all-to-all connectivity, but degrade to $O(\sqrt{N}\,\mathrm{polylog}\,N)$ for $N$ fermionic modes on 2D nearest-neighbor architectures. We present a fermionic permutation protocol tailored to 2D grid architectures that achieves the optimal $O(\sqrt{N})$ depth with $O(N\sqrt{N})$ nearest-neighbor gates and no ancilla qubits, mid-circuit measurements, or classical feedforward. title: Rounding Almost Commuting Hamiltonians
summary:
Commuting Hamiltonians lie at the boundary between classical constraint satisfaction and quantum many-body physics, exhibiting rich quantum structure while remaining more tractable than general noncommuting models. In contrast, physical Hamiltonians are rarely exactly commuting, which naturally motivates the study of almost commuting Hamiltonians. Despite their relevance, the implications of approximate commutation are only poorly understood.
  In this work, we show how to efficiently approximate any almost commuting $2$-local qubit Hamiltonian by a commuting one: we give a locality-preserving algorithmic rounding technique that maps any $2$-local Hamiltonian $H=\sum_{i=1}^m h_i$ with $\|[h_i,h_j]\| \leq ε$ to a nearby Hamiltonian $\hat{H}$ whose terms pair-wise commute, and which is within overall distance $\|H-\hat{H}\| = O(m\,ε^{1/6})$. As a consequence, we show that $δ$-approximations to the ground energy for $ε$-almost commuting $2$-local qubit Hamiltonians lie in $\mathsf{NP}$ when $δ\gg mε^{1/6}$, extending the classical containment well beyond the commuting setting. Finally, we present two applications of our rounding framework: Gibbs sampling and fast Hamiltonian simulation for almost commuting systems.
